definition: A maritime shipping term indicating that a vessel must remain buoyant at all times and is not permitted to intentionally ground, dry out, or take the bottom.
summary: Always Afloat is a rule in shipping that means a ship must stay floating on water and never sit on the seabed. This concept is important for safety, as grounding a vessel can cause damage and operational delays. It is considered in planning where the ship will dock, ensuring the berth has enough depth. Crew and port operators check the ship’s draft—the part of the hull under water—before loading or unloading cargo. Tides are also monitored, so ships move only when there is enough water to keep them afloat. The rule affects how much cargo a ship can carry, because too much weight might lower it into shallow water. Pilots and port authorities coordinate to make sure ships follow Always Afloat regulations. It is included in many shipping contracts to make responsibilities clear between charterers and vessel owners.

definition: A chartering term meaning that certain costs or responsibilities apply at both the load port and the discharge port.
summary: BENDS is a chartering term meaning that certain costs or responsibilities apply at both the load port and the discharge port. It is most commonly used in voyage charter parties to indicate that expenses such as port charges, pilotage fees, tug services, agency fees, or cargo handling costs are allocated to either the charterer or owner at both ends of the voyage. The term helps clarify which party is responsible for paying these costs during loading and unloading operations. It also defines how cost allocation is handled in the voyage settlement, reducing the potential for disputes. BENDS ensures that both ports are treated consistently with respect to charges and obligations, and it is often referenced in the charter party clauses relating to port expenses, duties, and operational responsibilities.
image_alt: Bends Diagram showing cost responsibility

definition: An electronic system used to exchange standardized commercial and logistics documents between parties without manual intervention.
summary: EDI, or Electronic Data Interchange, is a system that allows the electronic exchange of standardized commercial and logistics documents between trading partners without manual intervention. It is widely used in shipping, freight forwarding, and supply chain operations to transmit bills of lading, manifests, invoices, booking confirmations, purchase orders, and customs filings. The system reduces reliance on paper and manual data entry, improving both speed and accuracy in document handling. EDI also enhances compliance with international regulations by ensuring that transmitted documents follow standardized formats. It is integrated with carrier systems, port authorities, freight forwarders, and customs agencies to streamline the movement of goods. The technology supports automatic notifications and status updates, helping coordinate operations across multiple parties. Document transmission occurs in near real-time, reducing errors caused by delays or miscommunication. EDI messages are typically structured using widely accepted formats such as EDIFACT or ANSI X12. Workflow automation is enhanced, as routine document approvals, billing, and reporting can be processed without human intervention. Visual representations often include icons for computers, servers, shipping containers, and document flows showing the seamless exchange of information between parties.

definition: Always Accessible, Always Afloat is a port or berth condition stating that a vessel can access the berth at all times and can remain afloat without depending on tidal windows or intentionally touching the seabed. In practical terms, the vessel should be able to enter, remain alongside, and leave safely at any time.
summary: AAAA confirms that the berth, approach channel, and surrounding waters provides sufficient depth for the vessel’s draft throughout all stages of the call, including arrival,  berthing, cargo operations, and departure. This condition removes the need for tidal planning and reduces waiting time outside the port. It is commonly referenced when assessing berth suitability, especially for larger or deeper-draft vessels. AAAA provides assurance that cargo operations can proceed without interruption caused by low water levels. It is also used to compare ports and terminals when evaluating operational efficiency and risk. In chartering and voyage planning, the term helps clarify port capabilities and sets clear expectations regarding accessibility and safety.
image_alt: Visual representation of AAAA

definition: A port or chartering condition permitting a vessel to remain either continuously afloat or safely aground without risk of damage while alongside in port.
summary: Always Afloat or Safe Aground is used to define acceptable operating conditions at a berth or port. It allows a vessel either to remain fully afloat or to rest on the seabed in a controlled and safe manner. When safe aground is permitted, the seabed must be suitable, even, and free of hazards that could damage the hull. The vessel must be able to ground and refloat without structural stress or risk. This condition is commonly found in ports with large tidal ranges or shallow berths. Operational planning considers vessel type, hull strength, cargo distribution, and tidal patterns. The term helps clarify risk allocation and berth suitability in charter parties. It provides flexibility while ensuring that any grounding occurs only under safe and predictable conditions.
image_alt: Visual representation of AAS

definition: A major Northwest European shipping and trading region encompassing the ports of Amsterdam, Antwerp, and Rotterdam.
summary: The Amsterdam–Antwerp–Rotterdam Area, commonly referred to as ARA, is one of the most important maritime and trading regions in the world. It includes three major ports that serve as key gateways for cargo moving into and out of Europe. The area is heavily used for bulk commodities, tankers, containers, and breakbulk cargo. ARA is especially significant in the energy and commodities markets, as it is a major hub for oil, refined products, chemicals, coal, and agricultural cargoes. The region is frequently referenced in charter parties, freight negotiations, and bunker pricing. Storage capacity, terminal infrastructure, and hinterland connections make ARA a benchmark location for logistics and trading activities. Freight rates, port costs, and fuel prices are often quoted with direct reference to the ARA region. The term is used to describe the combined commercial influence of these ports rather than a single geographic port.

definition: A nautical term meaning located toward or at the rear (stern) of a vessel relative to another reference point.
summary: Abaft is used to describe the position of something relative to another point on a ship, specifically in the direction of the stern. When an object or space is said to be abaft another, it lies behind it along the vessel’s length. The term is commonly used in navigation, vessel descriptions, and onboard instructions to indicate relative location. For example, accommodation spaces, machinery, or cargo areas may be described as being abaft the bridge or abaft midships. Abaft does not describe distance, only direction, and is always referenced in relation to another feature on the vessel.

definition: A maritime term meaning physically present on or inside a vessel, aircraft, or other means of transport.
summary: Aboard is used to indicate that a person, cargo, or object is physically on or inside a vessel. In shipping and maritime operations, it commonly refers to crew members being present on the ship or cargo being loaded onto it. The term applies during all stages of a voyage, including loading, transit, and discharge. Instructions such as boarding personnel, placing equipment aboard, or confirming cargo aboard are standard operational uses. Aboard describes presence or placement rather than location within the vessel and is used broadly across navigation, operations, and documentation.

definition: A shipping term referring to cargo, equipment, or structures stowed or located on the deck of a vessel rather than within its holds.
summary: Above deck is used to describe cargo, equipment, or areas situated on the deck level of a vessel rather than inside enclosed holds. It commonly applies to containers, project cargo, deck machinery, and superstructure spaces. Items carried above deck are exposed to weather, sea spray, and wind, which affects stowage, lashing, and protection requirements. The term is frequently used in cargo descriptions, stowage plans, and operational instructions to distinguish between deck cargo and under-deck cargo. Above deck does not imply a specific position along the vessel’s length, only that the item is located on or above the deck surface.

definition: A logistics and shipping term describing the taking in or bearing of costs, capacity, or physical properties by a vessel, cargo, or party.
summary: Absorption is used in shipping and logistics to describe how something takes in or accommodates an impact, load, or obligation. In a commercial context, it often refers to costs being absorbed by an owner, charterer, carrier, or service provider rather than being passed on to another party. In cargo and vessel operations, absorption can describe how available space, weight capacity, or volume is taken up by cargo. The term is also used in a physical sense for materials or packaging that absorb moisture, vibration, or shock during transport. Its meaning depends on context and may appear in charter parties, freight calculations, cargo specifications, or commercial agreements. Absorption helps explain how capacity, risk, or cost is managed within an operation rather than transferred elsewhere.

definition: A commercial and shipping term indicating that a figure is approximate rather than exact.
summary: ABT is used in shipping and commercial documents to show that a quantity, date, weight, dimension, or rate is not fixed and may vary within a reasonable range. It commonly appears in charter parties, bills of lading, cargo descriptions, and freight agreements. The term allows for normal operational variations such as loading tolerances, measurement differences, or scheduling adjustments. By indicating approximation, ABT helps prevent disputes when minor deviations occur that are commercially acceptable and operationally unavoidable.

definition: The act by which a consignee or authorized party acknowledges receipt of goods as delivered and in apparent good order.
summary: Acceptance of Goods refers to the formal receiving of cargo, meaning the receiving party acknowledges they have taken the goods into custody or taken delivery of them. In shipping, this can occur when a carrier or terminal accepts cargo for transport, or when the consignee accepts cargo at destination. Acceptance often triggers key responsibilities such as care, custody, and control, and it can affect when risk transfers depending on the contract terms. It is typically evidenced by documentation such as a receipt, proof of delivery, delivery order, gate-in record, or a signed acknowledgement. After acceptance, claims for visible damage or shortages may need to be raised quickly, since the act of acceptance can be treated as confirmation that the goods were received in apparent good order unless exceptions are noted.

definition: A formal confirmation that goods, documents, or information have been received by the intended party.
summary: Acknowledgement of Receipt is used in shipping and logistics to confirm that cargo, paperwork, or electronic data has been received. It does not necessarily confirm the condition, accuracy, or completeness of what was received, only that receipt has occurred. The acknowledgement may be issued by a carrier, terminal, warehouse, consignee, or system, depending on the transaction. It is commonly evidenced by a signed document, electronic confirmation, timestamped system message, or delivery record. This acknowledgement is often used to establish a reference point for responsibility, timelines, or subsequent actions such as inspection, processing, or payment.

definition: The measured or realized demand for goods or services based on confirmed orders or actual consumption.
summary: Actual Demand in logistics refers to demand that has materialized through firm customer orders, sales transactions, or physical movement of goods. It reflects what is truly required by the market at a given time, as opposed to projected or forecast demand used for planning. Actual demand drives execution activities such as picking, packing, transportation, and replenishment. It is used to validate forecasts, adjust inventory levels, and measure planning accuracy. In supply chain operations, monitoring actual demand helps align production, warehousing, and distribution with real market needs.

definition: The definitive voyage number assigned to a vessel for an executed voyage as opposed to a provisional or planned reference.
summary: Actual Voyage Number is used in shipping and logistics systems to identify the voyage that physically took place, as opposed to a planned or provisional voyage number. It is assigned or confirmed once the vessel departs or the voyage is operationally fixed. The number is used across documentation, billing, tracking, reporting, and performance analysis. It links cargo movements, port calls, and operational events to the executed voyage. Using the actual voyage number ensures consistency between operational records and commercial or financial settlement.

definition: A notification issued to confirm that a specific operation or contractual obligation has been completed.
summary: Advice of Completion is used in logistics, shipping, and commercial operations to formally confirm that an agreed task has been finished. This may relate to cargo loading or discharge, delivery of goods, completion of a service, or fulfillment of a contractual obligation. The notice is typically issued by the performing party to the counterparty or stakeholder. It often serves as a trigger for subsequent actions such as invoicing, payment, documentation release, or closing of operational records. The advice establishes a clear completion point for operational and commercial reference.

definition: A commission paid to a charterer or intermediary, often at a nominal rate, as an allowance or rebate in a charter party.
summary: Address Commission is a fee paid to a broker or intermediary for introducing a charterer, owner, or cargo interest that results in a concluded transaction. It is typically agreed as a percentage of freight, hire, or lump sum and stated in the charter party or fixture recap. The commission compensates the intermediary for providing the business lead rather than for ongoing brokerage services. Payment terms, rate, and entitlement are usually defined contractually and settled alongside other voyage or hire accounts.

definition: The additional worth created by a product or service as a result of a specific process or activity.
summary: Added Value in logistics refers to improvements or services that increase the usefulness, efficiency, or commercial worth of goods or operations. This may include consolidation, packaging, labeling, kitting, inventory management, faster transit times, improved visibility, or risk reduction. Value can also be added through better coordination, cost optimization, or service reliability. In commercial terms, added value explains why a logistics service commands a premium beyond simple transportation. It is commonly referenced when comparing service offerings, supply chain strategies, or operational performance.

definition: An additional document or clause that supplements and forms part of an existing contract or agreement.
summary: An addendum is used in shipping, logistics, and chartering to introduce new terms or amend existing ones without rewriting the entire agreement. It may address changes such as revised rates, additional clauses, operational instructions, or updated responsibilities. The addendum forms part of the original contract once agreed and signed by the relevant parties. It is commonly referenced alongside charter parties, service contracts, and commercial agreements to reflect changes made after initial execution.

definition: An agreement between a shipper and a carrier governing communications and conditions prior to the tendering of a consignment.
summary: Advance Arrangement refers to understandings put in place before cargo is formally offered for carriage. It typically covers booking processes, documentation requirements, cargo details, timing, routing, and any special handling or regulatory conditions. These arrangements allow both parties to prepare operationally and commercially in advance of shipment. By setting expectations early, advance arrangements help reduce delays, last-minute changes, and disputes once the cargo is tendered. They are commonly used in regular trade lanes, contract logistics, and repeat shipment relationships.

definition: A sum of money paid in advance on behalf of or to a party prior to final settlement.
summary: An Advanced Amount is used in shipping and logistics to fund anticipated expenses before they are finally known or invoiced. It commonly covers costs such as port charges, bunker expenses, canal dues, or agency fees during a voyage or operation. The amount is paid ahead of time to ensure uninterrupted operations. Once final costs are determined, the advanced amount is reconciled against the final disbursement or account. Any balance is either refunded or adjusted in the settlement between the parties.

definition: A charge paid by a carrier to an agent or another carrier that is later collected from the consignee by the delivering carrier.
summary: Advance Charge refers to expenses initially paid by a carrier, agent, or intermediary to facilitate the movement of a shipment. These charges may include forwarding fees, handling costs, customs-related payments, or other incidental expenses incurred during transit. The amounts are advanced to avoid delays and ensure smooth execution of the shipment. At destination, the delivering carrier or agent collects these charges from the consignee as part of the delivery or arrival charges. Advance Charges are commonly used in air cargo, courier, and multimodal transport operations.

definition: An interline carrier that collects cargo from the shipper and delivers it to another carrier for onward transportation to the consignee.
summary: Advanced Interline refers to an arrangement where one carrier performs the initial pickup of cargo at origin and hands it over to a second carrier for the main leg of transportation. This structure is commonly used in air cargo and multimodal logistics networks where carriers cooperate to extend service coverage. The advanced interline carrier is responsible for origin handling, documentation handover, and timely transfer of the shipment. The receiving carrier then assumes responsibility for linehaul movement and delivery. This arrangement enables efficient routing across different carrier networks while maintaining continuity of the shipment.

definition: A written notification providing information about the status, movement, or handling of goods.
summary: An Advice Note is used in logistics and transport operations to communicate key updates related to a shipment. It may inform relevant parties about dispatch, arrival, delay, readiness for pickup, or changes in handling instructions. The document is informational in nature and does not transfer ownership or confirm receipt of goods. Advice notes help coordinate actions between shippers, carriers, terminals, warehouses, and consignees by keeping all parties aware of shipment status.

definition: The moment a vessel arrives at the first designated sea pilot station before entering a port or pilotage area.
summary: Arrival First Sea Pilot Station is used in shipping and chartering to establish a clear operational reference point before port entry. It marks the vessel’s arrival at the offshore location where a sea pilot boards or is scheduled to board the vessel. AFSPS is often referenced for the purpose of issuing notices of readiness, measuring time, or determining when contractual obligations such as laytime or demurrage may begin. It is particularly relevant at ports where pilot boarding occurs well outside the port limits and prior to navigating restricted waters.
image_alt: Visual representation of AFSPS

definition: The hiring of a vessel or vessels for the carriage of goods under agreed terms and conditions.
summary: Affreightment refers to an arrangement where a carrier agrees to transport cargo for a shipper in return for freight. The agreement may cover a single voyage, a series of voyages, or multiple shipments over a defined period. It does not necessarily involve the chartering of a specific vessel for exclusive use, but rather a commitment to carry agreed quantities of cargo. Affreightment is commonly structured through a Contract of Affreightment (COA), which sets out cargo volumes, loading and discharge ports, laytime terms, and freight rates. The concept is widely used in bulk, commodity, and liner trades where regular or repetitive cargo movements are required.

definition: A nautical term indicating a position toward the stern or rear of a vessel.
summary: Aft is used to describe the location of areas, equipment, or activities situated toward the back end of a ship. It provides a directional reference rather than a specific distance and is always understood in relation to the vessel’s orientation. The term is commonly used in navigation, vessel layout descriptions, cargo stowage planning, and operational instructions. Examples include references to aft accommodation, aft cargo spaces, or equipment located aft of midships. Aft helps ensure clear and unambiguous communication when coordinating shipboard operations.
image_alt: Visual representation of where aft of a vessel is

definition: A charge levied by an agent for services provided on behalf of a vessel, carrier, or cargo interest.
summary: Agency Fee refers to the remuneration paid to a shipping or port agent for acting on behalf of a vessel owner, operator, carrier, or cargo interest. These fees cover services such as coordinating port calls, handling documentation, arranging pilotage and tugs, managing crew matters, and liaising with port authorities, terminals, and service providers. Agency fees may be charged as a lump sum or as part of a detailed disbursement account. They are a standard component of port-related costs and are typically settled by the party responsible under the charter party or service agreement.

definition: Parties appointed to act on behalf of a principal in shipping, logistics, or transport-related matters.
summary: Agents act on behalf of shipowners, charterers, carriers, or cargo interests to manage operational and administrative activities. Their responsibilities commonly include handling documentation, coordinating port formalities, arranging services, and communicating with terminals and authorities. Agents facilitate smooth vessel calls and cargo movements by ensuring that regulatory, commercial, and operational requirements are met. Their role supports efficient turnaround and continuity of operations across ports and transport hubs.

definition: The total quantity of inventory held across multiple locations, facilities, or stages in the supply chain.
summary: Aggregate Inventory represents the combined stock held across warehouses, distribution centers, in-transit locations, or production stages. It is used to understand overall inventory exposure rather than focusing on individual sites. This view supports planning decisions related to replenishment, capacity utilization, service levels, and risk pooling. By analyzing aggregate inventory, organizations can balance stock availability against carrying costs and demand variability across the supply chain.

definition: A condition in which a vessel is resting on the seabed or bottom and is no longer fully afloat.
summary: Aground describes a situation where a vessel’s hull is supported by the seabed rather than by buoyancy alone. This may occur unintentionally due to navigation errors, low tides, or inadequate water depth, or intentionally at certain berths designed for controlled grounding. Whether being aground is acceptable depends on contractual and operational terms, such as Safe Aground or NAABSA, which define seabed suitability and vessel tolerance. When not permitted, grounding can lead to hull damage, delays, and liability issues. The term is commonly referenced in charter parties, port descriptions, and incident reporting.
image_alt: Visual representation of a vessel sitting on top of the seabed, no longer afloat

definition: The verified total weight of cargo including packaging and securing materials.
summary: Actual Gross Weight represents the full measured weight of a shipment as it is presented for transport. It includes the net weight of the cargo itself, the weight of packaging such as crates or pallets, and the weight of lashing, dunnage, or securing materials used to stabilize the cargo. When cargo is containerized, tare weight of the container is also considered separately to determine total container weight. Actual Gross Weight is used for stowage planning, load calculations, and regulatory compliance, including SOLAS Verified Gross Mass requirements. Accurate declaration of actual gross weight is essential for vessel stability, equipment limits, and transport safety.
image_alt: Visual representation of what actual gross weight is compared to net weight, tare weight and VGM

definition: An informal operational phrase indicating that a process, voyage, or operation is proceeding as expected without issues.
summary: All Going Well (AGW) is used in day-to-day shipping and logistics communications as a brief status update. It indicates that operations are progressing normally and that no problems, delays, incidents, or changes are currently affecting the plan. The phrase is often included in voyage reports, email updates, port call messages, and internal coordination notes. It reflects the situation at the time of reporting and may change if new developments arise.

definition: A vessel condition or cargo position located above the high load line marking.
summary:
Above High Load Line refers to a situation where a vessel’s draft or cargo position exceeds the high load line marking. Load lines are regulatory marks that indicate the maximum safe loading limits under various conditions. Operating above the high load line can affect vessel stability, seaworthiness, and safety margins. The term is used in stability assessments, compliance checks, and operational discussions to highlight potential regulatory or insurance concerns. Exceeding allowable load lines may result in restrictions, penalties, or refusal of port clearance.

Plimsoll Mark (Load Line Disc) – the circular mark on the ship’s hull that defines legal loading limits.
TF (Tropical Fresh Water) – maximum draft allowed in tropical fresh water.
F (Fresh Water) – maximum draft allowed in fresh water.
T (Tropical) – maximum draft allowed in tropical salt water.
S (Summer) – standard summer saltwater load line.
W (Winter) – reduced draft allowed in winter conditions.
WNA (Winter North Atlantic) – most restrictive load line due to severe sea conditions.
Above High Load Line (AHLL) – area above the applicable load line, indicating overloading beyond permitted limits.

definition: A vessel access standard referring to hold ladders fitted in accordance with Australian port and safety requirements.
summary:
Australian Hold Ladders refers to a specific standard for ladders installed inside cargo holds to provide safe access between deck level, hold coamings, and tank tops. These ladders are designed to meet Australian port authority and safety regulations, including requirements for angle, spacing, handholds, and landings. They are commonly referenced in charter parties and inspection checklists for vessels calling Australian ports. Properly fitted hold ladders allow safe entry for surveyors, stevedores, inspectors, and crew during cargo operations. Non-compliance can result in access restrictions, delays, or refusal of port operations.
Australian Hold Ladders became a commonly used shipping phrase because Australian ports (and the stevedoring environment) historically pushed for safer, more standardized access into cargo holds—especially on bulkers—where falls and unsafe access arrangements were recurring hazards.
image_alt: Ladder inside hold of a vessel per Australian standards.

definition: Structures or devices used to assist mariners in determining position and safe navigation.
summary: Aids to Navigation refer to the system of visual, electronic, and audible markers used to guide vessels along safe routes. These include buoys, beacons, lighthouses, leading lights, daymarks, and electronic aids such as AIS transmitters. They are used to mark channels, port approaches, shoals, wrecks, and other navigational hazards. Aids to Navigation are essential for safe port entry, coastal navigation, and confined-water operations. Their placement, color, shape, and light characteristics follow internationally recognized systems, allowing mariners to interpret them consistently across different regions.
image_alt: View from the bridge of a ship, showing navigation equipment inside the ship and buoys and lighthouse outside.

definition: A planning approach focused on optimizing inventory levels through forecasting and demand alignment.
summary: AIM is used in logistics and supply chain management to determine how much inventory should be held, where it should be positioned, and when it should be replenished. It relies on demand forecasts, consumption patterns, and lead-time analysis to balance product availability with inventory carrying costs. By improving visibility across warehouses and distribution networks, AIM supports better planning decisions, reduces excess stock, and helps maintain consistent service levels while controlling operational costs.

definition: Companies that design and produce automatic identification equipment used to identify, track, and exchange data between vessels and shore systems.
summary: Automatic Identification Manufacturers supply hardware and software for systems such as AIS that support vessel tracking, collision avoidance, and maritime situational awareness. Their products are used by shipowners, ports, and authorities to meet safety and regulatory requirements.

definition: The assignment of capacity, resources, or quantities to specific customers, cargoes, or services.
summary: Allocation is used in shipping and logistics to determine how limited capacity or resources are distributed among multiple demands. This may include allocating vessel space, containers, equipment, warehouse slots, or inventory quantities. Allocation decisions are often required during peak seasons, disruptions, or capacity shortages. The process helps balance customer commitments, operational constraints, and commercial priorities to ensure controlled and efficient use of available resources.

definition: A reserved portion of capacity or space assigned to a specific party or purpose.
summary: Allotment refers to an agreed reservation of space on a vessel, aircraft, or transport service that is held for a particular party over a defined period. It is commonly used in liner shipping and air cargo to provide certainty of capacity, especially on high-demand routes or during peak seasons. Allotments support better volume planning, smoother operations, and more predictable service levels for both carriers and shippers.

definition: A nautical term meaning located above the main deck or at a height on a vessel.
summary: Aloft refers to positions or work carried out above the main deck level, such as on masts, rigging, antennas, radar scanners, or communication equipment. The term is commonly used in operational instructions and safety procedures to describe activities performed at height. Being aloft carries additional safety considerations, including fall protection, permits to work, and restricted vessel movements. The term provides clear vertical reference when coordinating maintenance, inspections, or navigation-related tasks.

definition: The central portion of a vessel located midway between the bow and the stern.
summary: Amidships refers to the middle section of a vessel, positioned approximately halfway between the bow and the stern. This area is commonly used as a reference point in navigation, stability calculations, and vessel design because it represents the ship’s balance point. Cargo stowed amidships generally experiences less vertical and pitching motion compared to forward or aft sections. The term is also used when describing machinery spaces, accommodation blocks, and structural layout in ship plans.

definition: A designated area where vessels may anchor while awaiting instructions, berth availability, or clearance.
summary: Anchorage refers to a specified sea area where vessels are permitted to anchor instead of remaining underway or alongside a berth. These areas are designated and regulated by port or maritime authorities and may be used for waiting, bunkering, quarantine, inspections, or operational standby. Conditions at anchorage, such as weather, depth, and holding ground, are carefully considered to ensure vessel safety. Time spent at anchorage can have contractual implications, particularly in relation to laytime, demurrage, or readiness under charter party terms.
image_alt: A ship at sea with its anchor down, sitting in anchorage.

definition: A classification-approved system allowing continuous inspection of cargo transport units instead of periodic examinations.
summary: The Approved Continuous Examination Program is primarily applied to freight containers under international safety regulations. It allows containers to remain in service as long as they are regularly inspected and maintained according to an approved scheme. Instead of being withdrawn from service for mandatory interval inspections, containers under ACEP are examined during normal operations. This approach helps maintain structural integrity, improves compliance, and reduces downtime while ensuring safety standards are consistently met.

definition: An operational area where cargo, equipment, or vehicles are staged adjacent to transport infrastructure.
summary: An apron is a designated working area used for the handling, staging, and movement of cargo, equipment, or vehicles close to transport interfaces. In airports, it refers to the airside area where aircraft are parked for loading, unloading, refueling, and servicing. In terminals and logistics facilities, aprons provide space for positioning handling equipment and organizing cargo flows. Proper apron management is essential for safety, efficient operations, and minimizing turnaround times.
image_alt: Comparison pic showing aprons of a seaport and an airport

definition: A network of national information centres focused on information technologies.
summary: APRYCLEE refers to a cooperative framework that links national information centres involved in information technology exchange, coordination, or development. The term is generally used in institutional, administrative, or policy-related contexts rather than in day-to-day shipping or logistics operations. Its relevance depends on the specific organizational or regional framework in which it is referenced.

definition: A Northern European port range covering the major ports between Antwerp and Hamburg.
summary: ANTHAM is a shorthand used in shipping and chartering to describe a key Northwest Europe trading region. When a contract, rate, or market report mentions this range, it means the cargo or vessel can operate at any of the major ports in this corridor—commonly Antwerp, Rotterdam, Amsterdam, Bremen/Bremerhaven, and Hamburg—rather than a single named port. This gives operational flexibility and a standardized way to discuss pricing, availability, and market conditions across closely connected ports.

definition: A term referring either to a vessel’s equipment and fittings or, in logistics, to a single item of clothing transported as cargo.
summary: In maritime usage, apparel refers to a ship’s essential outfit—such as anchors, chains, rigging, lifeboats, and other fixed or required equipment needed for safe operation. In logistics and supply chains, apparel simply means clothing or garments being shipped, stored, or distributed, usually as part of retail or fashion cargo. The meaning is determined by context: ship operations versus cargo handling.

definition: The point at which a vessel arrives to embark or disembark a marine pilot.
summary: APS is a standard operational reference point in shipping. When a ship reaches the Arrival Pilot Station, a licensed pilot boards (or disembarks) to guide the vessel safely into or out of port. This point is often used in charter parties and port operations to mark arrival time, trigger notices, calculate laytime, and determine pilotage and port-related costs. For a layperson, it is essentially the ship’s official handover point to a local navigation expert.
image_alt: A pilot vessel in front of a container ship

definition: A Northwest European port range including Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Antwerp, and Ghent.
summary: ARAG is a commonly used shipping and chartering shorthand to describe a cluster of closely connected ports in Northwest Europe. It is broader than ARA, as it adds Ghent to Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and Antwerp. In practice, using ARAG in contracts or market discussions means the vessel or cargo can operate at any of these ports, allowing flexibility in routing, pricing, bunker supply, and scheduling across this regional hub.

definition: A designated location where maintenance or repair work on a container, vessel or equipment is carried out.
summary: Area of Repair is a formal reference used in operations, insurance, and technical documentation to specify where repairs are allowed or required. It helps define responsibility, compliance, and cost allocation, and may be restricted to approved yards, depots, or zones under class rules, port authority regulations, or insurance conditions. For a layperson, it simply means the approved place where something is fixed.

definition: A formal dispute resolution process in which a neutral arbitrator renders a binding decision.
summary: In shipping, arbitration is commonly specified in charter parties and contracts to settle disputes privately and efficiently. The parties agree in advance on the rules and venue (for example, London or New York), benefiting from confidentiality and decision-makers with maritime expertise. For a layperson, it means a private judge chosen by the parties decides the dispute, and the decision must be followed.

definition: A numeric or alphanumeric code identifying a specific geographic or operational area.
summary: Area Codes are used in logistics systems, telecommunications, and routing to classify regions for planning and reporting. They support standardization and data accuracy.Area Codes are applied in terminals, depots, and logistics systems to track container position and support yard planning and retrieval. They improve visibility and operational efficiency within storage and handling facilities.

definition: A contractual arrangement defining geographic areas where a vessel or asset is considered off-hire.
summary: Area Off-Hire Lease clauses specify locations where hire payments are suspended due to operational restrictions or non-availability. They are used to manage risk and cost exposure in leasing and chartering agreements.

definition: A lease agreement specifying geographic areas where an asset is deemed on-hire and hire charges apply.
summary: An Area On-Hire Lease establishes where and when hire accrues based on the asset’s location or operation within defined regions. It provides clarity for billing and operational responsibility.

definition: A notification issued to inform relevant parties that a vessel or cargo has arrived or is expected to arrive.
summary: An Arrival Notice is commonly sent by carriers or agents to consignees and notify parties of impending or actual arrival. It supports planning for customs clearance, delivery, and cargo receipt and does not in itself constitute delivery or acceptance.

definition: A European regulatory framework governing the transport of dangerous goods by road.
summary:
ADR establishes standardized rules for classifying, packaging, labeling, documenting, and handling hazardous materials transported by road across Europe. It applies to domestic and international movements and is especially relevant where road transport forms part of a multimodal supply chain. ADR is updated regularly to reflect technological advances, new substances, and safety lessons learned.

ADR was first adopted in 1957 under the auspices of the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) to harmonize the safe transport of dangerous goods by road between European countries. It entered into force in 1968 and has since expanded beyond Europe, with several non-European states also becoming contracting parties. The agreement is revised on a biennial cycle, ensuring consistent safety standards and alignment with other international dangerous goods regimes such as RID, IMDG Code, and ICAO Technical Instructions.

definition: A condition where a vessel is positioned next to a berth, quay, or another vessel for loading or discharge.
summary: Alongside is a standard operational and contractual term in shipping. It is used to indicate when a ship has reached its working position and is ready for loading or discharge. In charter parties and sale contracts, being alongside can trigger key events such as the start of laytime, transfer of risk, or delivery obligations. It is also commonly used to describe ship-to-ship operations where two vessels are secured side by side.
image_alt: A container vessel alongside the quay waiting for operations.

term: Association of Ship Brokers and Agents
aliases: association of ship brokers and agents
definition: A professional organization representing ship brokers, agents, and maritime service providers.
summary:
The Association of Ship Brokers and Agents, commonly known as ASBA, is a non-profit industry body that supports and regulates professional standards for ship brokerage and agency services. It develops widely used charter party forms, promotes ethical conduct, and provides arbitration services for maritime disputes.

ASBA is especially known for publishing standard charter party contracts (for example, the 'ASBATANKVOY' form for tanker voyages) and for administering maritime arbitration in New York. These contracts and dispute-resolution services are widely used in bulk and tanker trades calling US ports.

In chartering and brokerage practice, ASBA forms and arbitration clauses are common in bulk and tanker fixtures involving US interests. Its documentation and arbitration framework are considered industry standard in the New York maritime market.

definition: A chartering expression indicating that port operations can be carried out safely under prevailing conditions.
summary: ASPW is used in voyage communications, daily port reports, and Statements of Facts to confirm that prevailing weather, sea state, tidal range, labor availability, and terminal infrastructure permit normal cargo operations. When a port is declared ASPW, it indicates there are no safety-related impediments such as high winds, heavy swell, strikes, equipment breakdown, or berth restrictions affecting performance. This declaration is operationally significant in laytime and demurrage calculations, as time will typically continue to count while the vessel is able to work safely. If conditions later deteriorate and the port ceases to be ASPW, stoppages may be logged and evaluated under the applicable charter party clauses. The term therefore plays a practical role in documenting responsibility for delays and protecting the contractual position of owners and charterers.

definition: The process of combining parts, components, or goods into a complete or market-ready unit within a production or logistics environment.
summary: In logistics and supply chain operations, assembly refers to structured value-added activities where individual components are organized, fitted, or integrated to create a finished or semi-finished product. This may occur at manufacturing plants, third-party logistics warehouses, or distribution centers as part of postponement strategies. Assembly activities can include kitting, bundling, labeling, configuration, or light mechanical integration depending on the product complexity. Performing assembly closer to the end market reduces finished goods inventory exposure, improves responsiveness to demand variability, and supports product customization. From a cost and operational standpoint, it allows companies to optimize transport efficiency by moving components in bulk and completing final configuration nearer to the customer.

definition: The legal transfer of contractual rights and, where permitted, obligations from one party to another party.
summary: In shipping and commercial practice, assignment allows a party to transfer its contractual rights—such as freight earnings, hire receivables, or performance rights—to a third party. Obligations under the contract may only be transferred if the contract permits and the counterparty consents, as liabilities cannot typically be imposed on a new party without agreement. Assignment clauses are common in charter parties, lease agreements, and service contracts, often requiring prior written consent to remain valid. Proper documentation is essential to ensure continuity of rights, clarify liability exposure, and avoid disputes regarding performance or payment. In practice, assignment is frequently used for financing purposes, corporate restructuring, or commercial substitution of parties.

definition: A nautical term meaning behind or at the rear of a vessel.
summary: Astern is used in navigation and maneuvering to describe relative position or motion. Commands such as 'go astern' mean the vessel is moving backward, while positional references describe objects or vessels located behind the ship. It is a standard directional term in bridge operations and seamanship.
image_alt: A container vessel with arrow pointing towards the stern location and astern written on the back.

term: All Time Day and Night Sundays and Holidays Included
aliases: all time day and night sundays and holidays included
definition: A charter party laytime expression stating that all time counts continuously for laytime purposes, including nights, weekends, Sundays, and public holidays, without interruption.
summary: ATDNSHINC is a comprehensive laytime counting provision used primarily in voyage charter parties to ensure that time runs uninterrupted once laytime has commenced. Under this clause, there is no distinction between working days and non-working days; nights, Sundays, and public holidays are treated the same as regular weekdays. This maximizes time counting in favor of the party entitled to count laytime, typically the shipowner. It limits the charterer’s ability to exclude periods based on calendar status unless specific exceptions are separately agreed. In practical terms, once Notice of Readiness is validly tendered and laytime begins, every hour counts continuously until cargo operations are completed or laytime is otherwise contractually suspended.

definition: A nautical term describing a direction, alignment, or position that runs across the width of a vessel, from port side to starboard side.
summary: Athwartships refers to anything oriented laterally across a ship, perpendicular to the fore-and-aft (longitudinal) axis. The term is commonly used in naval architecture, stability calculations, and cargo stowage planning to describe transverse structures, bulkheads, beams, or cargo positioning. Proper athwartships distribution of weight is critical for maintaining transverse stability and preventing list. In cargo operations, equipment, lashings, or cargo units may be secured athwartships to control movement and balance. The term contrasts directly with fore-and-aft, which describes alignment along the vessel’s length.
image_alt: A breakbulk vessel with arrow pointing across its width indicating that is what athwartships mean.

definition: A laytime expression indicating that only the actual elapsed operational time is counted for contractual laytime or demurrage calculations.
summary: ATUTC clarifies that time calculations are based strictly on real, recorded operational periods rather than theoretical allowances or scheduled working hours. It is typically supported by the Statement of Facts and time sheets issued by the agent or terminal. Under this approach, only the time genuinely consumed in cargo operations or waiting periods counts toward laytime. It ensures transparency and accuracy in demurrage or dispatch assessments. The clause is applied where precise accountability of time is commercially significant.

definition: A commercial sales process in which goods are sold to the highest bidder through competitive offers.
summary: Auctions are commonly used to dispose of surplus inventory, used equipment, distressed cargo, or project assets. Buyers compete by submitting progressively higher bids within a defined time frame. This mechanism allows sellers to achieve market-driven pricing rather than fixed negotiated rates. In logistics and industrial sectors, auctions are frequently conducted online or at physical yards. They provide liquidity for hard-to-move or specialized assets while offering buyers potential value opportunities.

definition: A structured and independent examination of financial records, operational procedures, or compliance systems to assess accuracy and effectiveness.
summary: An audit evaluates whether processes and records conform to established standards, regulations, or contractual obligations. In logistics, audits may review freight billing, customs compliance, warehouse controls, or safety procedures. Financial audits verify accounting accuracy and internal controls. Operational audits assess efficiency, risk exposure, and process integrity. Findings are typically documented in a formal report with corrective recommendations.

definition: The process of confirming the identity of a user, system, or data source before granting access or validating information.
summary: Authentication ensures that only verified individuals or systems can access secured platforms, documents, or operational controls. In logistics and shipping environments, it protects cargo data, customs filings, and financial transactions. Methods include passwords, digital certificates, biometric scans, and multi-factor authentication. Strong authentication reduces fraud risk and unauthorized system manipulation. It is a foundational element of digital supply chain security.

definition: The formal granting of permission for a specific action, transaction, or operational activity.
summary: Authorisation establishes control by ensuring that actions are carried out only by duly approved individuals or entities. In logistics and maritime operations, it may apply to cargo release, payment approvals, charter fixtures, or system access rights. It creates accountability by linking responsibility to designated decision-makers. Authorisation frameworks are typically documented within company procedures or contractual clauses. Proper authorisation mitigates operational, financial, and compliance risks.

definition: A shipping container that is purpose-built or specially fitted (typically with vehicle racks, wheel chocks, and lashing points) to transport one or more motor vehicles safely and efficiently.
summary: Auto containers emerged as an adaptation of mainstream containerization rather than a single, standalone invention. After modern intermodal container shipping took off in the mid-1950s under pioneers like Malcom McLean and early containership operations, the industry moved toward standardized ISO container dimensions and fittings, making it practical to move high-value cargo—like vehicles—in closed, secure boxes. Over time, vehicle shippers progressed from simply loading one vehicle into a standard 20’/40’ container with lashings, to using purpose-designed in-container racking frames that allow multiple cars (often 2–4+ depending on size and container height) to be stacked and immobilized, improving utilization and reducing damage risk. This progression was driven by automotive supply chains, used-vehicle export lanes, and the need for better protection against weather, pilferage, and handling damage compared with some alternatives. 'Auto containers' as seen today were developed incrementally by logistics providers and equipment manufacturers through improved securing methods, modular racks, and standardized container interfaces.
image_alt: A side cross-sectional view of container showing 4 cars secured inside the container, two on the floor and two above, on a blue stand.

definition: A technology used to automatically identify and track objects or units through electronic data exchange.
summary: In maritime operations, Automatic Identification commonly refers to AIS (Automatic Identification System), which transmits vessel identity, position, speed, and course in real time. Ships exchange signals with other vessels and shore stations to enhance collision avoidance and traffic management. The system improves navigational safety, regulatory compliance, and situational awareness in congested waters. It is mandatory for most commercial vessels under international conventions.

definition: A maritime term describing loss, damage, or extraordinary expense incurred during a sea voyage.
summary: Average is primarily used in marine insurance and casualty contexts. It is classified as General Average, where losses are shared proportionally among all voyage interests, or Particular Average, where losses are borne by the individual party affected. The concept governs how financial responsibility is allocated following incidents such as fire, grounding, or jettison. It is a foundational principle in maritime risk allocation.

definition: Independent specialists who calculate and apportion losses and expenses arising from marine casualties.
summary: Average Adjusters are appointed following incidents involving General Average or significant insured losses. They review documentation, evaluate claims, and determine each party’s financial contribution. Their adjustment statements formally allocate costs among shipowners, cargo interests, and insurers. Their work ensures equitable and legally defensible settlement of maritime losses.

definition: A central high-capacity network that interconnects subsidiary networks and supports primary data transmission.
summary: A Backbone forms the core communication infrastructure of large IT environments. It carries high volumes of data between distribution centers, offices, cloud platforms, and logistics systems. Reliability and speed are critical, as disruptions impact multiple connected operations. In supply chain environments, backbone networks support real-time tracking, order management, and system integration.

definition: Information systems operating behind user interfaces to process transactions, manage data, and support operational workflows.
summary: Back End Systems manage core functions such as inventory control, billing, shipment processing, and financial reconciliation. They integrate with front-end platforms like customer portals and tracking interfaces. In logistics, they ensure data accuracy, regulatory compliance, and operational continuity. Without robust backend systems, real-time supply chain coordination would not be possible.

definition: The movement of cargo on the return leg of a transport route after completing an initial delivery.
summary: Back Haul maximizes asset utilization by reducing empty repositioning. Carriers often offer competitive rates to secure return cargo. It improves cost efficiency, reduces fuel waste, and enhances route profitability. In maritime and trucking sectors, effective backhaul planning strengthens overall network performance.

definition: A letter of indemnity issued by a shipper to obtain a clean bill of lading despite known cargo discrepancies.
summary: A Back Letter is typically requested when cargo condition would otherwise require adverse remarks on the bill of lading. The shipper provides indemnity to the carrier for potential claims arising from issuing a clean document. While commercially used in certain trades, it carries legal and insurance risks. Carriers must exercise caution, as courts may invalidate indemnities that conceal known defects.

definition: An order placed for goods that are temporarily unavailable and will be fulfilled once stock is replenished.
summary: Back Orders arise when demand exceeds current inventory levels. They are logged in order management systems and fulfilled in sequence once supply is restored. Persistent backorders may indicate forecasting inaccuracies or supply constraints. Managing them effectively is critical to maintaining service levels and customer satisfaction.

definition: A planning technique that begins with a required completion date and calculates backward to determine activity start times.
summary: Back Scheduling is commonly used where delivery deadlines are fixed and non-negotiable. Planners work backward from the target shipment or installation date to schedule procurement, production, and transport milestones. It supports just-in-time operations and deadline-driven projects. The method reduces idle time and aligns resources to meet committed delivery dates.

definition: The accumulation of outstanding orders or pending tasks that have not yet been completed.
summary: Backlog reflects demand exceeding current operational capacity. It may result from supply shortages, labor constraints, or unexpected demand surges. In logistics and manufacturing, backlog levels are monitored as performance indicators. Controlled backlog can indicate strong demand, while excessive backlog signals capacity or process inefficiencies requiring corrective action.

definition: A freight surcharge applied by carriers to compensate for fluctuations in marine bunker fuel prices.
summary: BAF is commonly used in liner shipping to adjust freight rates in response to changes in fuel costs. It is calculated based on fuel price indices and trade lane consumption assumptions. The surcharge is typically listed separately from base freight on invoices. It protects carriers from fuel market volatility while providing transparency to shippers. BAF mechanisms may be revised periodically depending on contractual terms and market conditions.

definition: The internal cubic capacity of a vessel’s cargo hold available for stowing baled, packaged, or general cargo.
summary: Bale Capacity measures the usable volumetric space within a cargo hold after deducting structural intrusions such as frames and stiffeners. It is expressed in cubic meters or cubic feet. This figure is relevant for light but bulky cargoes where volume, rather than weight, limits intake. It is normally lower than grain capacity because it reflects practical stowage conditions for packaged goods. Accurate bale capacity figures support effective voyage planning and cargo allocation.
image_alt: An empty vessel showing the space it has for cargo.

definition: The actual stowable cubic space within a cargo hold or container suitable for baled or packaged cargo.
summary: Bale Space represents the effective usable volume available after accounting for structural members, curvature, and obstructions inside the hold. It differs from grain space, which assumes loose bulk cargo filling all voids. Bale space is critical in calculating cargo intake for general cargo vessels and multipurpose ships. It directly influences freight calculations and stowage efficiency for packaged goods.
image_alt: A cargo-hold drawing showing bale space.

definition: Weight, typically water carried in dedicated tanks, used to maintain vessel stability, trim, and structural integrity when cargo weight is insufficient.
summary: Ballast ensures proper draft, stability, and safe maneuverability when a vessel is partially loaded or empty. Modern ships use ballast water systems to adjust trim and list during voyages. Ballast operations are governed by international environmental regulations due to risks of invasive species transfer. Proper ballast management is essential for safe navigation and compliance with maritime conventions.

images.alt: image showing ballast operations of a ship

definition: A lump-sum payment agreed in a charter party to compensate a vessel for repositioning in ballast to a loading port.
summary: Ballast Bonus is negotiated in voyage charters when a vessel must sail empty to reach the loading area. It offsets fuel costs, time, and opportunity expenses incurred before cargo loading begins. The amount reflects prevailing freight markets, distance to the loading port, and vessel availability. It is typically paid in addition to freight and documented within the charter party agreement.

definition: An organized structure of banks and regulated financial institutions that manage deposits, lending, payments, foreign exchange, trade finance, and settlement of monetary obligations between parties.
summary: The Banking System is the financial backbone of international trade and shipping. It enables buyers and sellers in different countries to transact securely through mechanisms such as wire transfers, letters of credit (L/C), documentary collections, bank guarantees, and escrow services. In maritime operations, banks facilitate freight payments, vessel financing, bunker payments, port disbursements, and cargo settlements. They also manage currency conversion and credit risk between counterparties who may not know each other. Without the Banking System, global trade would rely on direct trust and physical cash, which is impractical and high risk. In simple terms, it is the secure payment and credit network that makes international shipping commercially possible.

definition: A data identification system that uses printed machine-readable patterns (lines or squares) to encode shipment or product information for electronic scanning and tracking.
summary: Bar Coding is a core operational tool in logistics, warehousing, and port operations. Each barcode represents specific data such as shipment number, container reference, product code, or inventory ID. When scanned, the system automatically retrieves the associated information in a database, reducing manual entry errors and increasing speed. In shipping, barcodes are used on cartons, pallets, bills of lading, warehouse receipts, and sometimes container seals. This allows cargo to be tracked from origin warehouse to final delivery point with real-time visibility. Bar coding is the black-and-white pattern you see on products in stores—when scanned, it instantly identifies what the item is and where it belongs.

definition: A vessel charter arrangement in which the shipowner provides only the vessel itself, transferring full possession, control, and operational responsibility to the charterer for an agreed period.
summary: In a Bareboat Charter, the charterer takes over the ship as if they were the owner for the duration of the contract. The owner provides only the physical vessel. The charterer is responsible for crewing, insurance, maintenance, fuel, technical management, regulatory compliance, and commercial employment of the vessel. This structure is often used for long-term leasing, fleet expansion, or financing purposes. It allows companies to operate ships without purchasing them outright. For a non-industry person: it is similar to leasing a car without a driver—you are fully responsible for operating and maintaining it while you use it.

definition: A flat-bottomed cargo vessel designed primarily for transporting large volumes of goods on rivers, canals, and sheltered inland waterways.
summary: Barges are essential for moving bulk commodities such as grain, coal, aggregates, steel, and containers between inland terminals and major seaports. Because they operate on calm inland waters, they are built for high cargo capacity rather than speed. Barges are often pushed or towed by tugboats and can be connected in long formations to move large volumes efficiently. They offer lower transportation costs and reduced road congestion compared to trucks. In simple terms, a barge is like a floating platform used to move heavy cargo along rivers instead of highways.
image_alt: A slide showing various types of barges - dry, hopper, liquid, container, car-float, flat-deck, spud, crane and barrack barges.

definition: Vertical steel locking bars fitted to the doors of a shipping container that engage with locking cams to securely seal the doors, helping maintain a weather-tight closure and protect the cargo during transport.
summary: Container door bars are one of the primary security and sealing components of a shipping container. When the handles are rotated, the bars lock the door at multiple points, creating a tight seal that helps keep out rain, seawater, dust, and unauthorized access. They work together with the door gasket to maintain the container's weather-resistant integrity, although the gasket itself provides the actual watertight seal. Damaged or bent locking bars can prevent the doors from closing properly, increasing the risk of cargo damage, moisture ingress, or security issues.
image_alt: Shipping container door locking bars securing the container doors.

definition: The primary operating location or home depot where containers, trailers, or other transport equipment are stored, maintained, inspected, dispatched, and returned after use.
summary: A base is the central hub where containers, trailers, or transport equipment are managed throughout their operational life. It is the location where equipment is parked when not in service, inspected, repaired, cleaned, and prepared for its next assignment. Most logistics operations dispatch equipment from the base and return it there after deliveries are completed. An efficiently managed base improves equipment availability, maintenance planning, asset tracking, and overall fleet performance.

definition: The minimum inventory level maintained to satisfy expected demand during the time required to replenish stock.
summary: Basic stock is the inventory kept on hand to ensure normal operations continue while new supplies are being ordered and delivered. It is calculated to cover expected demand during the replenishment lead time and helps prevent disruptions caused by routine supply delays. Maintaining adequate basic stock reduces the risk of stockouts, improves customer service levels, and supports efficient inventory management without carrying excessive inventory.

definition: A group of products, materials, transactions, or data that are processed, manufactured, handled, or transported together as a single unit.
summary: A batch is a collection of similar items that are processed or managed together rather than individually. In manufacturing, a batch may consist of products made during the same production run, while in logistics it can refer to shipments or orders grouped for handling or transportation. Batch processing improves efficiency, reduces operating costs, and simplifies quality control and traceability. If a defect or issue is identified, the entire batch can be tracked, inspected, or recalled more easily.

definition: A specific quantity of goods produced, processed, packaged, or handled together as a single identifiable batch under the same production or handling conditions.
summary: A batch lot is a defined quantity of products that is manufactured or processed during the same production run and assigned a unique lot number for identification. Batch lots are essential for inventory control, quality assurance, and regulatory compliance because they allow products to be traced throughout the supply chain. If a quality issue or recall occurs, the affected batch lot can be quickly identified and isolated without impacting unrelated products. Batch lots are widely used in manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, food production, warehousing, and logistics.

definition: A manufacturing method in which identical products are produced in predetermined groups or batches rather than through a continuous production process.
summary: Batch production involves manufacturing a specific quantity of products before stopping production to switch to another product or batch. This approach provides flexibility to produce different products using the same equipment while maintaining consistent quality within each batch. It is commonly used in industries such as food processing, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, and consumer goods where production volumes vary or products require periodic changeovers. Batch production balances efficiency with customization, making it suitable for fluctuating demand and diverse product lines.

definition: Wooden or metal strips fixed to the inside walls of a vessel's cargo hold or a shipping container to keep cargo away from the sides, allowing air circulation and reducing moisture damage.
summary: Battens create a protective gap between the cargo and the walls of a vessel or container, allowing air to circulate freely and reducing the risk of condensation, mold, rust, and other moisture-related damage. They also help prevent cargo from rubbing directly against the steel walls, reducing the chance of physical damage during transit. Battens may be permanently installed as part of the vessel's structure or temporarily fitted depending on the type of cargo being carried. They are commonly used for moisture-sensitive cargo such as timber, paper products, machinery, and steel.
image_alt: Wooden battens installed along the inside walls of a shipping container to improve airflow and protect cargo from moisture and contact damage.

definition: A vertical section of a container vessel, measured from port to starboard, that is used to identify and organize container stowage positions along the ship's length.
summary: A bay is one of the primary reference points used in container vessel stowage planning. Bay numbers are assigned sequentially from the bow (front) to the stern (rear) to accurately identify where containers are loaded onboard. On most container ships, odd-numbered bays are used for 20-foot container positions, while even-numbered bays represent 40-foot container positions. Together with row and tier numbers, bay numbers form the complete container location reference used by ship planners, terminals, and carriers.
image_alt: Illustration showing container vessel bay numbering from bow to stern with odd-numbered 20-foot bays and even-numbered 40-foot bays.

definition: A diagram or electronic stowage plan showing the planned location of cargo or containers on a vessel using bay, row, and tier positions.
summary: A bay plan is the primary document used by vessel planners, terminals, and ship officers to determine where each container or cargo unit will be loaded onboard. It identifies every container's location by bay, row, and tier while also indicating container size, weight, type, hazardous cargo, and special handling requirements. Bay plans are essential for maintaining vessel stability, ensuring efficient loading and discharge operations, minimizing re-handling, and complying with safety and regulatory requirements throughout the voyage.
image_alt: Example bay plan showing container locations on a vessel using bay, row, and tier numbering.

definition: A freight payment condition requiring all freight and related charges to be paid before cargo discharge or unloading begins at the destination port.
summary: Before Breaking Bulk (BBB) is a shipping term that requires the consignee or its agent to pay all freight charges before the carrier begins discharging the cargo. This condition protects the carrier from the risk of non-payment by ensuring freight revenue is collected before delivery operations commence. BBB is commonly used in charter parties, bills of lading, and general cargo shipments where the carrier wants to minimize financial exposure. Once payment has been confirmed, cargo discharge can proceed in accordance with the vessel's operational schedule.

definition: The IMO Code of Safe Practice for Solid Bulk Cargoes, developed to provide safe procedures for the loading, carriage, and discharge of solid bulk cargoes by sea.
summary: The BC Code was established by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) to promote the safe transport of solid bulk cargoes and reduce the risk of cargo-related accidents at sea. It provided guidance on cargo classification, stowage, trimming, moisture content, loading, unloading, and ship safety. Although it has now been replaced by the International Maritime Solid Bulk Cargoes (IMSBC) Code, the term 'BC Code' is still commonly used in the maritime industry when referring to the predecessor code or historical requirements. Understanding the BC Code remains important when reviewing older shipping documents and industry references.

definition: A chartering and contractual term indicating that both the commencement date and the expiration date are included when calculating the applicable time period.
summary: Both Dates Inclusive (BDI) is commonly used in charter parties, shipping contracts, and commercial agreements to make it clear that the first and last dates of a specified period are both counted. This removes ambiguity when determining laydays, cancellation periods, payment deadlines, or contract validity. Using BDI helps prevent disputes over time calculations by ensuring all parties interpret the contractual period consistently.

definition: The maximum width of a vessel, measured at its widest point from the outer side of one hull to the outer side of the other.
summary: Beam is one of a vessel's principal dimensions and plays a critical role in ship design, stability, cargo capacity, and maneuverability. A wider beam generally provides greater transverse stability and allows for increased cargo space, although it may restrict access to certain ports, canals, locks, or berths with width limitations. Together with the vessel's length, draft, and depth, beam is an essential measurement used for ship construction, voyage planning, and port compatibility.
image_alt: Front view of a vessel showing the beam measured across the widest part of the hull.

definition: Located beneath the main deck of a vessel, including cargo holds, machinery spaces, tanks, and other enclosed compartments below the weather deck.
summary: 'Below' refers to any area situated beneath a vessel's main deck. Below-deck spaces are primarily used for cargo stowage, machinery, fuel and ballast tanks, storage areas, and crew or operational spaces depending on the vessel's design. These enclosed areas protect cargo and equipment from weather, seawater, and environmental exposure while contributing to the vessel's stability, safety, and efficient use of space during the voyage.
image_alt: Cutaway illustration of a vessel showing below-deck cargo holds, machinery spaces, and other compartments beneath the main deck.

definition: The longitudinal bending stress acting on a vessel's hull due to the unequal distribution of weight and buoyancy along its length, causing the hull to bend in either hogging or sagging conditions.
summary: Bending moment is one of the primary structural forces considered in ship design and cargo loading. It occurs because the vessel's weight and the upward buoyant forces are rarely distributed evenly along the hull, creating bending stresses that may result in hogging or sagging. Excessive bending moments can lead to structural fatigue, cracking, permanent deformation, or even hull failure if allowable limits are exceeded. Proper cargo distribution, ballast management, and continuous load monitoring are essential to keep bending moments within the safe operating limits established by the vessel's classification society.
image_alt: Diagram illustrating hogging and sagging bending moments on a vessel caused by the unequal distribution of weight and buoyancy.

definition: A designated location within a port, terminal, or harbor where a vessel is moored to load or discharge cargo, embark or disembark passengers, or carry out other port operations.
summary: A berth is a specifically assigned space alongside a quay, pier, jetty, or wharf where a vessel is secured during its stay in port. Each berth is designed with suitable depth, length, and cargo-handling facilities to accommodate particular vessel types and sizes. Efficient berth allocation minimizes vessel waiting time, improves cargo handling productivity, and reduces port congestion. Berth availability and infrastructure are key factors influencing vessel turnaround time, shipping schedules, and overall port efficiency.
image_alt: Container vessel securely moored alongside a port berth with cranes and cargo-handling facilities.

definition: A chartering and shipping term indicating that both loading and discharging operations are included in the stated freight rate, laytime, or contractual provision, unless otherwise specified.
summary: Both Inclusive (BI) is commonly used in charter parties and freight quotations to show that the quoted terms apply to both the loading port and the discharge port. For example, if laytime is stated as '5 days BI,' the allowed time covers both loading and discharging operations under the agreed terms. Using BI avoids misunderstandings about whether a condition applies to only one end of the voyage or to both. It provides clarity in contracts and helps all parties understand their operational and financial responsibilities.

definition: A formal agreement between two countries that establishes the rules, rights, and conditions under which transportation services, such as road, rail, air, or maritime transport, may operate between them.
summary: A Bilateral Transport Agreement allows carriers from two countries to move passengers or cargo across each other's borders under agreed conditions. These agreements typically specify operating rights, permit requirements, designated routes, vehicle standards, customs procedures, and other regulatory requirements. They help facilitate international trade by providing a clear legal framework for cross-border transportation while protecting the interests of both countries. Without such agreements, international transport operations may be restricted or require special authorization.

definition: An official document issued by a port or health authority certifying the health status of a vessel, its crew, passengers, and, where applicable, its cargo, confirming that it is free from known infectious diseases at the time of departure.
