summary: A Bill of Health was historically required by many ports before allowing a vessel to enter or discharge cargo, particularly during outbreaks of contagious diseases such as cholera, plague, or yellow fever. It helped authorities assess the risk of disease transmission and determine whether quarantine or other health measures were necessary. While modern international health regulations and electronic reporting have largely replaced the traditional Bill of Health, the concept remains important in maritime health and port state control procedures.

definition: A legal transport document issued by or on behalf of a carrier that serves as a receipt for the goods, evidence of the contract of carriage, and, when negotiable, a document of title to the cargo.
summary: The Bill of Lading is one of the most important documents in international shipping and trade. It confirms that the carrier has received the cargo in the stated condition, outlines the terms under which it will be transported, and may allow ownership of the goods to be transferred while the cargo is in transit. Depending on its type, a Bill of Lading can be negotiable or non-negotiable and is commonly used for customs clearance, trade finance, cargo release, and resolving disputes. Common variations include straight bills of lading, order bills of lading, bearer bills of lading, combined transport bills of lading, and sea waybills.

definition: A contractual provision contained in or incorporated into a Bill of Lading that defines the rights, obligations, responsibilities, and liabilities of the carrier, shipper, consignee, and other parties involved in the shipment.
summary: Bill of Lading clauses establish the legal terms under which cargo is transported and delivered. They commonly address issues such as carrier liability, freight payment, limitations of liability, dangerous goods, claims procedures, jurisdiction, force majeure, and dispute resolution. These clauses form part of the contract of carriage and are legally binding on the parties. Understanding them is essential because they determine how risks and responsibilities are allocated if cargo is lost, damaged, delayed, or subject to a dispute.

definition: A structured document that lists all the raw materials, components, parts, subassemblies, and quantities required to manufacture or assemble a finished product.
summary: A Bill of Material (BOM) acts as the complete recipe for building a product. It identifies every item needed, the quantity required, and often includes part numbers, descriptions, and assembly relationships. Manufacturers, procurement teams, and logistics providers use the BOM to plan purchasing, production scheduling, inventory management, costing, and quality control. An accurate BOM helps ensure that the correct materials are available at the right time, reducing production delays and costly errors.

definition: The role of a Bill of Materials (BOM) in defining, organizing, and managing all components, materials, and assemblies required to manufacture a finished product throughout the production process.
summary: The Bill of Materials function serves as the foundation for manufacturing, procurement, inventory management, and production planning. It links engineering design with purchasing and shop-floor operations by specifying exactly what materials are needed, in what quantities, and how they fit together. A well-maintained BOM helps ensure accurate material planning, cost estimation, production scheduling, and inventory control while reducing errors, delays, and waste. It also provides traceability and consistency throughout the product's lifecycle, from design and manufacturing to maintenance and replacement parts.

definition: The world's largest international shipping association, representing shipowners, operators, brokers, agents, and other maritime stakeholders, and known for developing widely used standard shipping contracts and industry guidance.
summary: BIMCO - Baltic and International Maritime COuncil - plays a leading role in the global maritime industry by creating standard charter parties, bills of lading, clauses, and other contractual documents used in international shipping. It also provides legal guidance, market analysis, training, and operational best practices to help members navigate commercial and regulatory challenges. Many shipping contracts around the world are based on BIMCO's standardized forms, making them an important part of day-to-day maritime operations and international trade.

definition: A specially designed trailer that can operate on both highways and railway tracks, allowing cargo to move between road and rail transport without unloading or transferring the goods.
summary: A bimodal trailer combines the flexibility of road transport with the efficiency of rail transport in a single unit. Instead of unloading cargo from a truck to a rail wagon, the trailer itself is adapted for rail movement using specialized rail bogies or running gear. This reduces cargo handling, lowers the risk of damage, shortens transit times, and improves overall transport efficiency. Bimodal trailers are commonly used in intermodal and combined transport systems where seamless movement between road and rail is important.
image_alt: Illustration of a bimodal trailer operating on a highway and on railway tracks using rail bogies, demonstrating seamless road-to-rail intermodal transport.

definition: A document issued by a carrier or freight forwarder confirming that cargo space has been reserved on a specific vessel or voyage based on the shipper's booking request.
summary: A booking note is the first formal confirmation that a shipment has been accepted for transportation. It outlines the agreed shipment details, including the cargo, vessel, voyage, ports, freight terms, and cut-off dates. Although it is not a document of title, it serves as the agreement between the shipper and the carrier before the cargo is handed over for shipment. The information in the booking note is later used to prepare the shipping instructions and Bill of Lading.

definition: A person who assists with the berthing, mooring, unmooring, and movement of vessels within a port, terminal, or harbor.
summary: A boatman is responsible for helping vessels safely arrive at or depart from a berth by handling mooring lines and assisting with docking operations. They often work from the quay or from small workboats and coordinate with pilots, tugboats, and the ship's crew during vessel movements. Their role helps prevent damage to ships, port facilities, and mooring equipment while ensuring safe and efficient port operations.

definition: The most favorable commercial proposal a party is willing to make during negotiations, usually representing its final or most competitive price and terms.
summary: A best offer is typically submitted after negotiations have progressed and indicates the lowest price or most favorable terms a seller, carrier, or service provider is prepared to accept. In shipping and chartering, it may include freight rates, laycan, payment terms, and other commercial conditions. While a best offer demonstrates serious intent to conclude a deal, it is not binding until both parties formally accept and execute the agreement.

definition: A strong, fixed post installed on a quay, pier, jetty, dolphin, or vessel that is used to secure mooring lines and hold a vessel safely in position.
summary: A bollard provides a secure anchoring point for mooring lines during berthing and unberthing operations. It is designed to withstand the large forces created by a vessel's weight, wind, waves, currents, and tidal movements. Bollards are found both ashore and on board vessels in various shapes and sizes depending on the expected mooring loads. They are one of the most important pieces of mooring equipment, helping keep vessels safely alongside while protecting the ship, berth, and port infrastructure.
image_alt: Infographic showing quay and vessel bollards used to secure mooring lines during berthing operations.

definition: A Latin term meaning 'in good faith,' referring to actions, statements, agreements, or intentions that are honest, genuine, and made without fraud or deception.
summary: Bona fide is commonly used in shipping, logistics, legal, and commercial transactions to indicate that a party is acting honestly and with legitimate intent. A bona fide offer, buyer, supplier, or claim is one that is genuine and made without the intention to mislead or deceive. The term is frequently used in contracts, chartering negotiations, insurance, and international trade to distinguish legitimate business dealings from fraudulent or bad-faith actions.

definition: The status of imported goods kept under customs control in an approved bonded facility, where import duties and taxes are suspended until the goods are released for local consumption, exported, re-exported, or destroyed under customs supervision.
summary: Bonded goods are stored in approved customs-controlled facilities without the immediate payment of import duties and taxes. This allows importers to defer duty payments until the goods enter the local market, while goods that are re-exported, or destroyed under customs supervision may avoid import duties altogether. The goods must remain under customs control and cannot be sold, used, altered, or removed without authorization. Bonded storage supports cash-flow management, inventory planning, and lawful international trade.
image_alt: Infographic showing bonded goods stored under customs control until duties are paid, the goods are re-exported or they are destroyed under customs supervision.

definition: The process of reserving cargo space with a carrier or freight forwarder for the transportation of goods on a specific voyage, flight, train, or truck.
summary: A booking is the first formal step in arranging the transportation of cargo. It confirms that the carrier has accepted the request to transport the shipment, subject to agreed rates, schedules, equipment availability, and terms and conditions. Once the booking is confirmed, it serves as the basis for shipment planning, cargo acceptance, documentation, and the subsequent issuance of transport documents such as the Bill of Lading or Air Waybill. Accurate booking information helps ensure the cargo is moved on the intended service without delays.

definition: A unique identification number assigned by a carrier, freight forwarder, or logistics provider to a confirmed cargo booking for tracking and operational purposes.
summary: A booking reference number uniquely identifies a shipment reservation throughout the transportation process. It is used by carriers, freight forwarders, terminals, customs brokers, and shippers to retrieve booking details, track shipment status, coordinate cargo handling, and prepare transport documents. The reference number links the booking to operational systems and is commonly required when submitting shipping instructions, making inquiries, or checking the progress of a shipment.

definition: A stage, resource, or activity within a process that restricts the overall flow of work because its capacity is lower than the demand placed upon it.
summary: A bottleneck occurs when one part of a logistics or supply chain process cannot handle the volume of work passing through it, causing delays to everything that follows. Bottlenecks can occur at ports, warehouses, customs inspections, loading docks, transportation links, or production facilities. Identifying and eliminating bottlenecks improves throughput, reduces congestion, lowers costs, and increases the overall efficiency of the supply chain.
image_alt: Infographic illustrating a logistics bottleneck where cargo flow is restricted at one point in the supply chain, creating congestion and delays.

definition: Conical steel fittings installed on a vessel's deck that engage with a container's corner castings to secure the container in position and prevent movement during a voyage.
summary: Bottom fittings provide the foundation for securing shipping containers on board a vessel by locating and supporting the container's corner castings. They are commonly used together with twistlocks to prevent containers from shifting, lifting, or sliding due to rolling, pitching, vibration, and heavy seas. Properly installed bottom fittings help maintain the integrity of container stacks, protect cargo from damage, and contribute to the overall stability and safety of the vessel. They are a critical component of a ship's container securing system.
image_alt: Infographic showing conical bottom fittings installed on a vessel's deck engaging a shipping container's corner castings with twistlocks to prevent movement during a voyage.

definition: A container handling method in which lifting equipment engages the four bottom corner castings of a container to safely raise, move, or position it.
summary: Bottom lifting is a container handling technique commonly used in ports, terminals, depots, and inland logistics operations where specialized lifting attachments engage the container's bottom corner castings. Unlike conventional container handling with a top spreader, bottom lifting uses dedicated lifting beams, slings, or bottom-lift devices to support the container from below. This method is particularly useful where overhead clearance is limited or where specialized lifting equipment is required, ensuring safe, stable, and controlled container movement.
image_alt: Infographic showing a shipping container being lifted using equipment attached to the four bottom corner castings, illustrating the bottom lift handling method.

definition: The forward-most part of a vessel, designed to move through the water with minimum resistance while protecting the ship from waves and sea conditions.
summary: The bow is the front section of a vessel and is engineered to cut through the water efficiently, reducing drag and improving fuel economy. Its design plays a major role in a vessel's speed, stability, maneuverability, and ability to operate safely in rough seas. Different vessel types use different bow designs, such as bulbous, plumb, or axe bows, depending on their intended service and operating conditions. The bow also houses important equipment such as anchors, mooring gear, and navigation lights.
image_alt: Infographic showing the bow as the forward-most part of a vessel, illustrating its location, purpose, common bow designs, and its role in improving efficiency and seakeeping.

definition: A pallet fitted with fixed, removable, or collapsible side walls that form a box-like structure for containing, protecting, and transporting goods.
summary: A box pallet combines the handling advantages of a standard pallet with the added protection of enclosed sides. It is commonly used for transporting loose, fragile, or irregularly shaped goods that could shift or fall from a conventional pallet. Box pallets improve load stability, protect cargo from damage during storage and transport, and can often be stacked or folded when empty to save space. They are widely used in warehousing, manufacturing, distribution, and closed-loop logistics systems.
image_alt: Infographic illustrating a box pallet with side walls used to contain and protect cargo during storage, handling, and transportation.

definition: The commencement of cargo discharge operations from a vessel, marking the official start of unloading activities in port.
summary: In port operations, break bulk refers to the moment cargo discharge officially begins, which is an important operational milestone for calculating laytime, demurrage, and dispatch under many charter parties. The term is also commonly used to describe the handling of non-containerized general cargo, such as machinery, steel, timber, pipes, project cargo, and bagged goods that are loaded and discharged individually rather than in containers. The intended meaning is usually determined by the context in which the term is used.
image_alt: Infographic illustrating break bulk as the commencement of cargo discharge from a vessel and its association with non-containerized general cargo handling.

definition: Cargo that is transported as individual units rather than in containers or in bulk, with each piece loaded, stowed, secured, and discharged separately.
summary: Breakbulk cargo includes goods such as heavy machinery, steel products, pipes, timber, vehicles, project cargo, and bagged or palletized cargo that cannot be economically containerized or moved as bulk commodities. Because each item may differ in size, shape, and weight, breakbulk shipments require specialized lifting equipment, careful stowage planning, proper lashing, and skilled cargo handling. This type of cargo is commonly carried on multipurpose and heavy-lift vessels and is widely used in construction, energy, mining, and industrial projects.
image_alt: Infographic illustrating breakbulk cargo being loaded and discharged as individual units, with examples including machinery, steel, pipes, timber, vehicles, and project cargo.

definition: The quantity of fuel remaining in a vessel's bunker tanks at a specific point in time.
summary: Bunker on Board (BOB) refers to the amount of fuel a vessel has available for propulsion and onboard operations. It is commonly measured when a vessel is delivered to or redelivered from a charter, arrives or departs a port, or at the end of a voyage. The quantity of BOB directly affects voyage costs and is often included in charter party settlements, where the charterer pays for the fuel remaining on board or is reimbursed for the fuel consumed. Accurate BOB measurements are important for fuel management, voyage planning, and financial reconciliation.

definition: The quantity of fuel remaining in a vessel's bunker tanks at a specific point in time, typically measured in metric tons.
summary: BROB (Bunkers Remaining on Board) represents the amount of fuel left on a vessel at a defined reporting point, such as the completion of a voyage, vessel delivery, redelivery, or port arrival and departure. It is a critical figure in charter party performance, voyage accounting, and financial settlements, as it determines the value of fuel transferred between parties. Accurate BROB measurements help verify bunker consumption, support operational planning, prevent disputes, and ensure transparent settlement of fuel costs.

definition: Unusable cargo space within a vessel, container, or other cargo compartment resulting from the shape, size, or nature of the cargo being stowed.
summary: Broken stowage refers to the empty spaces that remain after cargo has been loaded because the available space cannot be completely filled. It is commonly encountered when loading irregularly shaped, oversized, or heavy cargo, where gaps are unavoidable to ensure safe stowage and proper weight distribution. Excessive broken stowage reduces the effective cargo-carrying capacity of a vessel, increases transportation costs per unit of cargo, and requires careful stowage planning to minimize wasted space while maintaining safety and cargo integrity.
image_alt: Infographic comparing efficient cargo stowage with broken stowage, illustrating unusable spaces created by irregularly shaped cargo and their impact on vessel capacity.

definition: An independent intermediary who brings together two or more parties to negotiate and arrange commercial transactions without taking ownership of the goods or services involved.
summary: A broker acts as a facilitator between buyers and sellers, shippers and carriers, or shipowners and charterers to help conclude commercial agreements. In the shipping industry, brokers commonly arrange vessel charters, freight bookings, vessel sales and purchases, or cargo movements, providing market knowledge and negotiating terms on behalf of their clients. Brokers are typically compensated through a commission or brokerage fee when a transaction is successfully concluded, but they do not assume ownership or operational responsibility for the cargo or vessel.

definition: The commission or fee paid to a broker for successfully arranging or negotiating a commercial transaction between parties.
summary: Brokerage is the compensation earned by a broker for bringing parties together and facilitating the successful conclusion of a commercial agreement. In shipping, brokerage is commonly paid for charter parties, vessel sale and purchase transactions, freight agreements, and other maritime contracts. It is typically calculated as an agreed percentage of the contract value or freight and is payable only in accordance with the terms of the underlying agreement or charter party.

definition: A former international customs tariff classification system developed by the Customs Cooperation Council (now the World Customs Organization) to provide a standardized method for classifying goods traded internationally.
summary: The Brussels Tariff Nomenclature (BTN) was introduced in 1959 to promote uniform customs classification and facilitate international trade by providing a common tariff language for participating countries. It formed the basis for customs duties, trade statistics, and tariff negotiations in many parts of the world. In 1988, the BTN was replaced by the Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System (Harmonized System or HS), which is now the internationally accepted standard used by customs administrations worldwide.

definition: A technical specification or standard published by the British Standards Institution (BSI) that establishes uniform requirements for the design, manufacture, testing, quality, safety, and performance of products, materials, and services, including freight containers.
summary: BSI Specifications are developed to ensure products and processes meet consistent technical, quality, and safety requirements. In the freight container industry, BSI standards helped establish uniform specifications for container construction, dimensions, materials, testing, and performance before the widespread adoption of international ISO container standards. Although ISO standards now dominate global container manufacturing, BSI standards continue to be used across many industries within the United Kingdom to support quality, safety, and regulatory compliance.

definition: The agreed terms, conditions, or reference point that define how a contract, quotation, freight rate, or transport service is to be interpreted and performed.
summary: Basis (BSS) specifies the assumptions and conditions under which a commercial or transport agreement is made. It may define factors such as the point of delivery, freight terms, quantity, measurement, loading or discharge conditions, or other contractual obligations that determine each party's responsibilities. Clearly stating the basis helps avoid misunderstandings, ensures both parties interpret the agreement consistently, and provides a reference for resolving disputes if they arise.

definition: A contractual transport basis under which the carrier's responsibility extends only from one named port of loading to one named port of discharge.
summary: BSS 1/1 defines a shipment that moves between a single loading port and a single discharge port. Under this basis, the carrier's responsibility is generally limited to the ocean transportation between those two ports, while inland collection, delivery, and any additional transport services are excluded unless specifically agreed in the contract. Clearly stating a BSS 1/1 basis helps establish the scope of the carrier's obligations, simplifies freight quotations, and avoids misunderstandings regarding responsibility for inland transportation.

definition: Charter party terms under which loading and/or discharge operations are performed only after the vessel has reached and is safely berthed alongside the designated berth.
summary: Under Berth Terms (BT), the vessel must arrive at and be securely alongside the nominated berth before cargo operations and, in most cases, laytime can commence, subject to the charter party terms. Delays caused by berth congestion or the unavailability of the berth generally remain the responsibility allocated under the contract until the vessel reaches the berth. Berth Terms are commonly contrasted with Port Terms, where obligations may begin once the vessel has arrived within the port limits rather than at the berth itself.
image_alt: Infographic explaining Berth Terms (BT), showing a vessel alongside a berth, when laytime commences, the operational implications, and how Berth Terms differ from other charter party loading and discharge terms.

definition: A floating aid to navigation that is permanently anchored to the seabed and used to mark channels, hazards, safe water, or other important navigational positions.
summary: A buoy is a floating marker that assists mariners in navigating safely by identifying channels, fairways, isolated dangers, safe water, anchorage areas, and other navigational information. Buoys are secured to the seabed by chains or cables and remain in a fixed position despite tides and currents. They are identified by standardized colors, shapes, topmarks, and lights in accordance with the International Association of Marine Aids to Navigation and Lighthouse Authorities (IALA) system, enabling vessels to navigate safely during both day and night.
image_alt: Infographic illustrating different types of navigational buoys, including lateral, cardinal, isolated danger, safe water, and special-purpose buoys, and explaining their role in aiding safe marine navigation.

definition: Commercial transactions conducted between businesses rather than between a business and individual consumers.
summary: Business-to-Business (B2B) refers to commercial activities where one company sells products or services to another company. B2B transactions are the foundation of logistics, shipping, manufacturing, and global supply chains, often involving larger shipment volumes, long-term contracts, negotiated pricing, and specialized services. Unlike Business-to-Consumer (B2C) transactions, B2B relationships typically focus on operational efficiency, reliability, and ongoing commercial partnerships.

definition: Inventory held in reserve to protect against supply disruptions, delivery delays, unexpected increases in demand, or other uncertainties in the supply chain.
summary: Buffer stock is maintained to reduce the risk of stockouts and ensure business operations continue when actual demand or supply differs from forecasts. It provides a safety margin against supplier delays, transportation disruptions, production issues, seasonal fluctuations, and unexpected customer demand. Maintaining an appropriate level of buffer stock improves service levels and operational continuity, although excessive buffer stock can increase inventory carrying costs and tie up working capital.

definition: Large flexible containers made from woven polypropylene fabric and used for the storage, handling, and transportation of dry bulk materials.
summary: Bulk Bags, also known as Flexible Intermediate Bulk Containers (FIBCs), are widely used for transporting and storing commodities such as grains, fertilizers, chemicals, minerals, powders, and food ingredients. They are lightweight yet capable of carrying loads ranging from several hundred kilograms to over one metric ton, making them a cost-effective alternative to rigid containers. Equipped with lifting loops for handling by forklifts or cranes, bulk bags simplify loading, unloading, storage, and transportation while reducing packaging waste and handling costs.
image_alt: Infographic illustrating Flexible Intermediate Bulk Containers (FIBCs), showing their construction, handling methods, common types, benefits, and typical uses for transporting and storing dry bulk materials.

definition: Cargo transported in large quantities without individual packaging, loaded directly into a vessel's cargo hold, tank, silo, or other storage unit in its loose, granular, powder, or liquid form.
summary: Bulk cargo consists of homogeneous commodities shipped without individual packaging and is generally classified as either dry bulk or liquid bulk. Dry bulk cargo includes commodities such as coal, grain, iron ore, fertilizers, cement, and salt, while liquid bulk cargo includes crude oil, petroleum products, chemicals, edible oils, LNG, and LPG. Because these commodities are handled in large volumes, they require specialized vessels, terminals, storage facilities, and loading and unloading equipment to ensure safe, efficient, and economical transportation.
image_alt: Infographic illustrating bulk cargo transportation, comparing dry bulk and liquid bulk commodities, the specialized vessels and terminals used to handle them, and the typical cargo handling process.

definition: A merchant vessel specifically designed to transport unpackaged dry bulk cargo in large cargo holds.
summary: Bulk carriers are purpose-built ships designed to transport dry bulk commodities such as coal, grain, iron ore, bauxite, cement, fertilizers, and other loose cargoes. Their large cargo holds, hatch covers, and robust hull structures allow them to carry high-volume cargoes safely and efficiently over long distances. Bulk carriers are classified by size, including Handysize, Supramax, Panamax, Capesize, and Valemax, and they play a vital role in supporting global commodity trade and industrial supply chains.
image_alt: Infographic illustrating a bulk carrier, its cargo holds, major vessel classes, typical dry bulk cargoes, ship features, cargo handling process, and its role in global commodity transportation.

definition: A freight container specially designed or modified to transport dry or liquid bulk cargo without the need for individual packaging.
summary: Bulk containers enable commodities such as grains, powders, pellets, chemicals, minerals, and other bulk products to be transported using standard containerized logistics networks. They are typically fitted with loading hatches, discharge outlets, liners, or hopper systems that allow cargo to be loaded and unloaded efficiently while minimizing contamination, product loss, and handling costs. Bulk containers combine the advantages of bulk transportation with the flexibility, security, and worldwide compatibility of ISO container transport.

definition: A vertical partition or wall within a vessel, container, or other structure that divides it into separate compartments for structural support, cargo separation, and safety.
summary: Bulkheads are essential structural components that divide a ship into separate compartments, increasing hull strength and helping to contain flooding, fire, or cargo movement if an incident occurs. In cargo spaces, bulkheads separate different cargoes, improve load distribution, and reduce the risk of shifting during a voyage. Depending on their purpose, bulkheads may be watertight, weathertight, fire-resistant, or designed for cargo segregation, making them a critical feature of modern vessel safety and construction.
image_alt: Infographic illustrating bulkheads inside a ship, showing how vertical partitions divide cargo holds and compartments to improve structural strength, limit flooding, segregate cargo, and enhance vessel safety.

definition: Heavy-duty metal rings permanently fitted to a vessel deck, truck or trailer bed, railcar, container floor, or other cargo-carrying surface. They serve as strong attachment points for chains, wire ropes, straps, or other securing equipment used to hold cargo in position during transportation. Bull rings are particularly useful when securing heavy, oversized, or irregularly shaped cargo that cannot rely on standard container securing methods.
summary: Bull rings are part of a cargo securing system and help prevent cargo from sliding, shifting, tipping, or becoming loose while in transit. Lashings are connected between the cargo and the bull rings to restrain movement caused by vessel motion, braking, acceleration, turns, or vibration. Their strength, location, and the securing equipment used with them must be suitable for the weight and forces generated by the cargo.
image_alt: Illustration showing bull rings used as attachment points for securing heavy cargo with chains or lashings

definition: Bundling is the practice of grouping two or more separate items together so they can be handled, transported, stored, or sold as a single unit. In logistics, items may be secured together using straps, bands, shrink wrap, pallets, or other packaging methods. This makes individual pieces easier and safer to handle while reducing the number of separate units that must be moved.
summary: Bundling improves handling efficiency by allowing several items to be managed as one consolidated unit. It can reduce handling time, packaging requirements, transportation costs, and the risk of individual pieces becoming separated or lost. Common examples include pipes strapped together, cartons secured on a pallet, or several products packaged together for distribution.
image_alt: Illustration showing common logistics bundling methods including strapped cartons, palletized goods, shrink-wrapped cargo, and bundled products

definition: Bunker refers to the fuel carried or supplied to a vessel for operating its main engines, auxiliary engines, boilers, and other onboard machinery. Common bunker fuels include Very Low Sulphur Fuel Oil (VLSFO), Heavy Fuel Oil (HFO), Marine Gas Oil (MGO), and Marine Diesel Oil (MDO). In everyday shipping usage, the word can refer both to the fuel itself and, historically, to the spaces where a ship's fuel was stored.
summary: The term originates from coal bunkers used on steamships. Today it refers to liquid fuels consumed during vessel operations. Bunker fuel is one of the largest operating costs for most commercial vessels, so its price, quality, and consumption have a major effect on voyage economics. The vessel must receive the correct quantity and specification of fuel because poor-quality or contaminated bunkers can damage machinery or disrupt operations. Bunker selection and consumption also affect a vessel's compliance with international air-emission and fuel-sulphur requirements.
image_alt: Infographic showing marine bunker fuel being transferred from a bunker barge to a cargo vessel through a fuel hose

definition: Bureau Veritas is an international classification society and testing, inspection, and certification organization. In shipping, it develops technical rules and standards used to assess the design, construction, condition, and maintenance of vessels and marine equipment. Surveyors inspect ships and review technical documentation to confirm that applicable class requirements and statutory regulations are being met.
summary: A vessel classed by Bureau Veritas has been assessed against the society's technical standards and is subject to continuing surveys throughout its operating life. Classification helps shipowners, insurers, charterers, flag states, and other parties understand whether a vessel meets recognized standards for structural integrity, machinery, and safety. Bureau Veritas also performs statutory surveys and certification when authorized by flag administrations, supporting regulatory compliance and safe maritime operations.
image_alt: Infographic showing a marine surveyor inspecting a commercial vessel and reviewing classification documents as an example of Bureau Veritas vessel classification services

definition: Business logistics is the planning, coordination, and control of how goods, materials, services, and related information move through a company. It covers activities such as transportation, warehousing, inventory management, order processing, packaging, and distribution. The goal is to make sure the right product reaches the right place, in the right quantity and condition, at the required time while controlling cost.
summary: Business logistics connects the different operational activities that move products from suppliers through the business and ultimately to customers. Good logistics management helps reduce unnecessary transportation, storage, and inventory costs while improving reliability and customer service. It also gives businesses better visibility over stock, deliveries, and supply requirements so they can respond more effectively to changes in demand or disruptions.

definition: Business Process Re-Engineering is the fundamental review and redesign of existing business processes to achieve major improvements in efficiency, cost, speed, quality, or customer service. Rather than making small adjustments to an existing workflow, BPR examines whether the process itself should be reorganized or replaced. It often involves eliminating unnecessary steps, changing responsibilities, automating activities, and using technology to create a more effective way of working.
summary: BPR is used when an organization wants significant improvement rather than gradual optimization. A company may redesign processes such as order handling, procurement, invoicing, warehousing, or customer service to reduce delays, duplication, and operating costs. Successful BPR can improve productivity and service quality, but it usually requires careful planning because it may significantly change established roles, systems, and workflows.

definition: A buyers market is a market condition in which the supply of goods, services, or available capacity is greater than the demand from customers. Because sellers are competing for fewer buyers, customers usually have more choices and stronger negotiating power. In logistics and shipping, this can occur when there is more vessel, truck, warehouse, or freight capacity available than the market requires.
summary: In a buyers market, prices and freight rates generally come under downward pressure because suppliers compete more aggressively for business. Buyers may be able to negotiate better rates, longer payment terms, improved service conditions, or more flexible contracts. The situation usually continues until demand increases or excess capacity is removed from the market.

definition: Brackish Water Arrival Draft is the vessel's draft measured upon arrival in water that contains a mixture of fresh water and seawater. Because brackish water is less dense than normal seawater, a vessel of the same displacement will generally sit slightly deeper in the water. The actual water density therefore needs to be considered when evaluating the vessel's draft against port, berth, or load line limitations.
summary: BWAD is particularly relevant at ports located in estuaries, rivers, and other areas where seawater mixes with fresh water. The measured draft may require a density correction, commonly considered through dock water allowance calculations, when comparing it with the equivalent seawater draft. Correctly accounting for this difference helps determine safe under-keel clearance, allowable draft, and compliance with port restrictions.
image_alt: Illustration comparing vessel draft in seawater and brackish water, showing the vessel sitting slightly deeper in the lower-density brackish water

definition: Cash Against Documents is a payment arrangement in which the buyer must make payment before receiving the shipping or title documents needed to take control of the goods. The seller ships the cargo and sends the relevant documents, often through a bank or appointed agent, with instructions to release them only after payment is received. These documents may include the bill of lading, commercial invoice, packing list, and other documents required for customs clearance or delivery.
summary: CAD gives the seller greater payment protection because control of the shipping documents is retained until the buyer pays. It is generally less secure than a letter of credit because the bank usually acts only as a document-handling intermediary and does not guarantee payment. For the buyer, payment is made after shipment has taken place but before the documents needed to obtain the cargo are released.

definition: Currency Adjustment Factor is a surcharge or adjustment applied to freight rates to compensate for changes in currency exchange rates. Carriers may collect freight in one currency while paying operating expenses in another, creating financial exposure when exchange rates fluctuate. CAF helps reduce the impact of these currency movements on the carrier's transportation costs.
summary: CAF is commonly associated with liner shipping and may be expressed as a percentage of the base freight rate or incorporated into the overall freight charge. The amount can increase or decrease depending on exchange-rate movements and the carrier's pricing methodology. It is generally reviewed periodically and may vary by trade route, carrier, and currency exposure.

definition: The visit of a vessel to a port.
summary: A call includes arrival, berthing, cargo operations, and departure. Port calls are scheduled as part of a vessel’s voyage rotation.

definition: A unique identification code assigned to a vessel for radio communication.
summary: Call signs are used in maritime and aviation communications. They ensure clear and unambiguous vessel identification.

definition: A collaborative network evaluating the exchange and use of digital technical information using CALS standards.
summary: The CALS Test Network brings together industry and government organizations. It demonstrates interoperability and standardized digital information use.

definition: The maximum amount that can be carried, stored, or processed.
summary: Capacity applies to vessels, terminals, warehouses, and systems. Managing capacity is essential for efficiency and cost control.

definition: The management of available capacity to match demand.
summary: Capacity control optimizes utilization and prevents congestion or underuse. It is critical in shipping, warehousing, and transport planning.

definition: Goods carried by a vessel, aircraft, truck, or train.
summary: Cargo may be bulk, breakbulk, containerized, or liquid. Its nature determines handling, documentation, and transport requirements.

definition: The physical movement of cargo during loading, discharge, and transfer.
summary: Cargo handling includes lifting, stowing, and securing goods. Proper handling reduces damage and improves operational safety.

definition: A code indicating limitations or special conditions applicable to certain cargo.
summary: Restriction codes highlight safety, regulatory, or operational constraints. They guide carriers and terminals in proper handling.

definition: A system or reference used to track the location and status of cargo.
summary: Cargo tracers provide visibility throughout the transport chain. They support planning, customer service, and exception management.

definition: A single item or consolidated unit handled as one piece of cargo.
summary: Cargo units may include pallets, containers, or packages. Standardization improves efficiency and traceability.

definition: The act of transporting goods from one place to another.
summary: Carriage may involve one or multiple transport modes. Responsibilities are defined by contracts and transport documents.

definition: An Incoterm where the seller pays carriage and insurance to the named destination.
summary: Risk transfers to the buyer when goods are handed to the first carrier. CIP requires insurance cover for the buyer’s benefit.

definition: An Incoterm where the seller pays transport costs to the named destination.
summary: Risk passes to the buyer upon delivery to the first carrier. CPT can be used for any mode of transport, including multimodal.

definition: A party that undertakes or procures the transport of goods.
summary: Carriers may operate by sea, air, road, rail, or inland waterways. They are responsible according to the contract of carriage.

definition: Inland transport arranged and performed by the carrier.
summary: Carrier haulage integrates inland movement with main transport. It offers a single point of responsibility for the shipper.

definition: Ports specified in a carrier’s bill of lading as load and discharge locations.
summary: These ports define the contractual scope of carriage. Deviations may require additional agreement.

definition: The carrier’s right to retain goods until freight and charges are paid.
summary: A lien protects the carrier against non-payment. It is exercised in accordance with contract and law.

definition: The temperature at which cargo must be maintained during transport.
summary: Carrying temperature is critical for perishable and sensitive goods. It is monitored throughout the journey.

definition: Short-distance transport of goods, usually by road.
summary: Cartage commonly covers movement between terminals and nearby facilities. It is a component of inland logistics.

definition: The process of normalizing product data from multiple suppliers for comparison.
summary: Catalog aggregation enables buyers to compare complex products. It is common in electronic marketplaces and virtual distribution.

definition: Entities that aggregate and normalize catalogs from multiple suppliers.
summary: They help buyers compare offerings while remaining neutral intermediaries. Revenue is generated through fees and value-added services.

definition: A unit of volume measurement equal to one meter in length, width, and height.
summary: CBM is used to calculate cargo volume using the formula length × width × height in meters. One CBM equals 1,000,000 cubic centimeters, 35.3147 cubic feet, and 61,023.7 cubic inches.

definition: A unit of volume measurement equal to one foot in length, width, and height.
summary: CBFT is calculated as length × width × height in feet. One CBFT equals 28,316.8 cubic centimeters, 0.0283168 cubic meters, and 1,728 cubic inches.

definition: A document that formally attests to a fact or compliance with requirements.
summary: Certificates are issued by authorized bodies. They are widely used in trade, transport, and regulatory processes.

definition: A document certifying the chemical or physical properties of goods.
summary: It is commonly used for chemicals, food, and pharmaceuticals. The certificate confirms compliance with specifications.

definition: A document confirming a vessel’s class with a classification society.
summary: It verifies compliance with structural and safety standards. The certificate is essential for operation and insurance.

definition: A document confirming that goods have been delivered.
summary: It provides evidence of receipt by the consignee. The document supports settlement and claims handling.

definition: A document confirming that goods are freely sold in the exporting country.
summary: It is often required for pharmaceuticals and consumer goods. The certificate supports regulatory approval abroad.

definition: A document certifying the country of origin of goods.
summary: Certificates of origin are used for customs and trade agreements. They may affect duty rates and eligibility.

definition: A document confirming the return of a vessel or equipment to the owner.
summary: It is used at the end of charters or leases. The certificate records condition and timing.

definition: An Incoterm where the seller pays cost and freight to the destination port.
summary: Risk transfers to the buyer once goods are loaded onboard. Insurance is not included under CFR.

definition: A facility where cargo is consolidated or deconsolidated into containers.
summary: CFS operations support LCL shipments. They are key nodes in container logistics.

definition: A mechanical system using chains to move goods along a fixed path.
summary: Chain conveyors are used in warehouses and terminals. They enable continuous and controlled cargo movement.

definition: Marketplaces that support existing distribution channels rather than replacing them.
summary: They maintain trader relationships outside the platform. Channel enablers facilitate transactions and data exchange.

definition: An amount payable for carriage or related services.
summary: Charges may be based on rates, weight, volume, or special services. They form part of total transport cost.

definition: A classification identifying the nature of a charge.
summary: Charge types distinguish freight, surcharges, and ancillary fees. They support transparency and accounting.

definition: A map used by navigators to plan and conduct voyages.
summary: Charts show depths, hazards, and navigational aids. They are essential for safe navigation.

definition: A contract for the hire of a vessel or part of its capacity.
summary: Charter parties define rights, obligations, and payment terms. They are fundamental documents in tramp shipping.

definition: The party that hires a vessel under a charter party.
summary: Charterers pay hire or freight to use the vessel. Their responsibilities depend on the charter type.

definition: A wheeled frame used to transport containers or forming the base of a vehicle.
summary: Chassis enable inland movement of containers. In vehicles, they support mechanical components.

definition: A contractual option exercisable at the charterer’s discretion.
summary: CHOPT allows flexibility within agreed limits. It is commonly used in voyage and time charters.

definition: The rate at which customers are lost and replaced over time.
summary: High churn reduces long-term value. It is a key metric in digital and service-based markets.

definition: An Incoterm where the seller pays cost, freight, and insurance to the destination port.
summary: Risk transfers once goods are loaded onboard. Insurance is arranged by the seller for the buyer’s benefit.

definition: The use of computer systems to integrate manufacturing processes.
summary: CIM links design, production, and logistics. It improves efficiency and data consistency.

definition: Goods shipped in disassembled form for later assembly.
summary: CKD reduces transport costs and duties in some markets. It is common in automotive and machinery trade.

definition: A contract for the carriage of a specified quantity of cargo over a period.
summary: COAs provide volume and rate certainty. They are commonly used for bulk commodities.

definition: A demand for compensation due to loss, damage, or delay.
summary: Claims arise from transport incidents. They are handled under contract and insurance terms.

definition: The process of assigning a vessel to a class based on technical standards.
summary: Classification ensures structural and operational safety. It is conducted by classification societies.

definition: An organization that sets and verifies standards for vessel construction and operation.
summary: Classification societies issue class certificates. They play a central role in maritime safety.

definition: A bill of lading stating that goods were received in apparent good order and condition.
summary: Clean bills facilitate trade and financing. They indicate no visible damage or defects at loading.

definition: A notation confirming goods were loaded onboard in apparent good condition.
summary: It is often required under letters of credit. The notation supports payment and title transfer.

definition: A terminal where goods are cleared by customs authorities.
summary: Clearance terminals handle inspection and documentation. They enable lawful import or export.

definition: A status indicating customs clearance without issues.
summary: CWE confirms full compliance with requirements. Goods may proceed without restriction.

definition: A party having a commercial relationship with a company for services or transport.
summary: Clients may engage directly or through agents. The relationship is governed by contract.

definition: A detachable refrigeration unit for temperature-controlled containers.
summary: Clip on units provide cooling without integral machinery. They are used for flexible reefer operations.

definition: A closed container fitted with ventilation openings.
summary: These containers allow air circulation while protecting cargo. They are used for goods requiring ventilation but not refrigeration.

definition: A group of buyers or sellers jointly operating a shared marketplace.
summary: Coalitions concentrate purchasing or selling power to increase transaction volume. They aim to improve pricing leverage and liquidity. Governance, regulatory, and system integration challenges are common.

definition: A container owned by the shipping line.
summary: Carrier owned containers are supplied and controlled by the ocean carrier. They are included in freight arrangements. Responsibility for availability and maintenance rests with the carrier.

definition: An empty space separating compartments on a vessel.
summary: Cofferdams isolate cargo spaces from machinery or tanks. They enhance safety by preventing leakage and contamination. They are common in tankers and bulk vessels.

term: Carriage of Goods by Sea Act
definition: A law governing rights and liabilities in sea carriage of goods.
summary: COGSA sets carrier responsibilities and limitations of liability. It standardizes bill of lading terms. The act is widely applied in international shipping.

definition: A container designed to be folded when empty.
summary: Collapsible containers reduce empty repositioning costs. They save storage space when not in use. They are common in automotive and retail logistics.

definition: A freight rate made up of multiple individual charges.
summary: Combination charges aggregate transport and service costs. They simplify billing for complex movements. Transparency of components remains important.

definition: A chassis adaptable to different container sizes.
summary: Combination chassis can handle 20, 40, or extended containers. They improve equipment flexibility. This reduces fleet size requirements.

definition: Transport using more than one mode under a single contract.
summary: Combined transport integrates sea, road, rail, or inland waterways. Liability is covered under one agreement. It improves logistics efficiency.

definition: A bill of lading covering transport by multiple modes.
summary: This document evidences a single contract for the entire journey. It simplifies documentation. It is widely used in door-to-door shipments.

definition: A document evidencing a multimodal transport contract.
summary: CTDs function similarly to bills of lading. They may be negotiable or non-negotiable. They support integrated logistics chains.

definition: A party responsible for combined transport under one contract.
summary: The CTO assumes responsibility across all transport legs. Risk transfers at contract level. This simplifies claims handling for shippers.

definition: A document detailing the sale of goods between buyer and seller.
summary: The commercial invoice is used for customs clearance. It states value, description, and terms of sale. Accuracy is critical for duty assessment.

definition: The use of goods or resources.
summary: Consumption measures demand within a supply chain. It influences inventory planning. Accurate tracking supports forecasting.

definition: A document detailing how cargo is arranged within a container.
summary: The container load plan specifies cargo positioning, weight distribution, and securing methods. It supports safe transport and efficient unloading. It is commonly used by shippers, warehouses, and carriers.

definition: A French container shipping company.
summary: CNC operates containerized maritime transport services. It is historically associated with regional and feeder shipping. The company has been integrated into larger carrier groups.

definition: A charter agreement covering the carriage of specified cargo over multiple voyages.
summary: This contract commits a shipowner to transport agreed quantities over time. It provides flexibility compared to voyage charters. COACP is commonly used for bulk and project cargo.

definition: The end of a standard business day.
summary: COB is used as a deadline reference in contracts and communications. It clarifies cut-off times for instructions and payments. The exact time depends on local business practices.

definition: The end of the business day in London.
summary: COBLDN is commonly used in finance and shipping contracts. It defines a time reference tied to the London market. This avoids ambiguity across time zones.

definition: A container owned by the shipping line.
summary: Carrier owned containers are supplied and controlled by the ocean carrier. They are included in freight arrangements. Responsibility for availability and maintenance rests with the carrier.

definition: A payment method where goods are paid for upon delivery.
summary: COD requires the consignee to pay before receiving the goods. It reduces seller credit risk. The method is common in domestic and courier shipments.

term: Carriage of Goods by Sea Act
definition: A law governing rights and liabilities in sea carriage of goods.
summary: COGSA sets carrier responsibilities and limitations of liability. It standardizes bill of lading terms. The act is widely applied in international shipping.

definition: The practice of combining cargo from multiple shippers into one container.
summary: Co-loading improves container utilization. It reduces freight costs for smaller shipments. Coordination between parties is essential to avoid delays.

definition: A cooperative relationship between manufacturers or partners.
summary: Co-makership focuses on long-term collaboration. It emphasizes trust, shared planning, and efficiency. The concept supports integrated supply chains.

definition: A product traded in commerce.
summary: Commodities may be raw materials or finished goods. They are often standardized. Pricing is influenced by market supply and demand.

definition: A flat freight rate for a specific commodity per container.
summary: Commodity box rates simplify pricing. They apply regardless of weight within limits. They are common in liner shipping.

definition: A numerical code classifying goods for customs purposes.
summary: Commodity codes determine duties and restrictions. They are harmonized internationally. Incorrect coding can cause penalties and delays.

definition: A local intermediary acting on behalf of a foreign firm.
summary: Compradores facilitate local transactions. They bridge cultural and commercial gaps. The role is common in historical and emerging markets.

definition: A malicious program designed to disrupt computer systems.
summary: Computer viruses can damage data and operations. They spread through networks or files. Cybersecurity controls are essential in logistics systems.

definition: A container equipped with a detachable refrigeration unit.
summary: Conair containers allow flexible temperature control. The cooling unit can be removed when not needed. They are used for perishable cargo.

definition: Rules governing contractual obligations.
summary: Conditions define rights and responsibilities of parties. They are integral to transport contracts. Clear conditions reduce disputes.

definition: Devices used to position and secure containers.
summary: Cones fit into container corner castings. They prevent movement during transport. They are essential for safe stowage.

definition: An accumulation causing delays in movement or handling.
summary: Congestion increases transit times and costs. It often occurs at ports or terminals. Capacity planning helps mitigate its impact.

definition: Short-distance road transport linking other transport modes.
summary: Connecting road haulage moves cargo between ports, terminals, and depots. It is a critical intermodal link. Efficiency affects overall transit time.

definition: The party to whom goods are shipped.
summary: The consignee receives the cargo at destination. They may or may not be the buyer. Their details appear on transport documents.

definition: Goods shipped under a single transport document.
summary: A consignment may include one or more packages. It is tracked as one shipment. Liability and documentation apply at consignment level.

definition: Directions provided for handling and delivering cargo.
summary: These instructions guide carriers and agents. They cover routing, documentation, and delivery terms. Accuracy ensures smooth execution.

definition: A document evidencing receipt of goods for transport and the terms of carriage.
summary: The consignment note accompanies cargo during transport. It provides shipment details, parties involved, and handling instructions. It is commonly used in road, rail, and multimodal transport.

definition: Inventory held by a consignee but owned by the consignor until sold or used.
summary: Consignment stock reduces upfront cost for the buyer. Ownership remains with the supplier until consumption. It requires accurate inventory tracking and clear contractual terms.

definition: The party who dispatches goods for transport.
summary: The consignor initiates the shipment and provides shipping instructions. They may be the seller or exporter. Their details appear on transport documents.

definition: To combine multiple shipments into one load.
summary: Consolidation improves transport efficiency and reduces cost. It is common for LCL and small consignments. Proper planning is required to avoid delays.

definition: A container holding cargo from multiple shippers.
summary: Consolidated containers maximize space utilization. They are typical in less-than-container-load operations. Coordination between shippers and consolidators is essential.

definition: The process of combining multiple shipments into one transport unit.
summary: Consolidation reduces freight cost per shipment. It improves equipment utilization. It is widely used in freight forwarding.

definition: A location where shipments are combined for onward transport.
summary: Consolidation points act as hubs in logistics networks. Cargo is sorted, grouped, and dispatched. They improve routing efficiency.

definition: A party that combines shipments from multiple shippers.
summary: Consolidators arrange groupage and shared containers. They negotiate transport rates with carriers. Their role is common in international forwarding.

definition: An association of companies cooperating for mutual benefit.
summary: In shipping, consortia share vessels and capacity. They reduce operating costs and expand service coverage. Members remain legally independent.

definition: An invoice certified by a foreign consulate.
summary: Consular invoices are required by some countries for customs clearance. They verify shipment value and origin. Their use has declined but still applies in certain trades.

definition: A standardized unit for transporting goods.
summary: Containers enable efficient multimodal transport. They protect cargo and simplify handling. Standard sizes allow global interchangeability.

definition: A supporting frame used to carry containers on rail wagons or trailers.
summary: Container bolsters distribute container weight evenly. They secure containers during transport. They are common in rail operations.

definition: A number used to validate a container identification code.
summary: The check digit ensures the container number is correctly recorded. It is calculated using a standard formula. This reduces errors in documentation and tracking.

definition: A facility for storage, maintenance, and handling of containers.
summary: Container depots manage empty and laden containers. They perform inspection and repairs. Depots support efficient container circulation.

definition: A contractual arrangement under which containers are rented for use over a specified period.
summary: Container leasing allows carriers and shippers to use containers without owning them. It provides flexibility in fleet size and reduces capital expenditure. Lease terms define duration, condition, and return location.

definition: The planning, control, and positioning of containers and related equipment.
summary: Container logistics ensures containers are available where and when needed. It involves repositioning empties, tracking movements, and optimizing utilization. Effective control reduces costs and shortages.

definition: A document detailing the contents of a specific container or transport unit.
summary: The container manifest lists cargo items, weights, and packing details. It is prepared by the party loading the container. The document supports customs, safety, and operational control.

definition: The number of container handling actions performed by a crane in a given period.
summary: Container moves are used as a productivity metric in terminals. Higher move counts indicate operational efficiency. They are often measured per hour or per shift.

definition: A unique identification code assigned to a container consisting of prefix, serial number, and check digit.
summary: The container number enables global tracking and documentation. It follows ISO standards for consistency. Accurate recording is essential for logistics and customs processes.

definition: The party that owns a container and has the right to lease or sell it.
summary: Container owners may be carriers, leasing companies, or other entities. Ownership determines responsibility for maintenance and asset management. Owners generate revenue through leasing or resale.

definition: A container floor without side or end walls used for oversized or heavy cargo.
summary: Container platforms allow loading by spreader directly from above. They are commonly used in Lo-Lo operations. Such units accommodate cargo that cannot fit standard containers.

definition: A shared stock of containers jointly used by multiple carriers or leasing companies.
summary: Container pools improve equipment availability and reduce empty repositioning. Participants share access under agreed rules. Pooling increases operational flexibility.

definition: A four-letter code identifying the owner of a container.
summary: The prefix forms the first part of the container number. It is registered internationally. This code links the container to its legal owner.

definition: An international convention establishing safety standards for containers.
summary: The CSC sets uniform requirements for container construction and inspection. It enhances safety in handling and transport. Compliance is mandatory for international trade.

definition: The numerical part of a container number identifying the specific container unit.
summary: The serial number distinguishes one container from another under the same prefix. It includes a check digit for validation. This ensures accurate identification.

definition: Fees payable by cargo interests for container-related services.
summary: These charges cover handling, storage, and related services. They are published in tariffs. Payment is required according to agreed terms.

definition: A two-digit code indicating the nominal length and height of a container.
summary: The size code is part of ISO container identification. It supports planning and stowage. Standardization ensures compatibility across transport modes.

definition: A standardized description of a container’s size and type under ISO 6346.
summary: This code identifies both dimensions and container design. It supports global interchange. Accurate coding is essential for equipment planning.

definition: Two or more containers placed vertically one above another.
summary: Stacks are common in terminals and depots. They optimize yard space. Safe stacking depends on weight and container condition.

definition: An agreement allowing a carrier to provide containers to another carrier for a fixed period.
summary: Sub-leasing improves container utilization. Terms define duration, payments, and responsibilities. It supports network flexibility.

definition: A facility where containers are loaded, discharged, and transferred.
summary: Container terminals handle vessel, rail, and truck operations. They provide storage and handling services. Terminals are critical nodes in supply chains.

definition: A two-digit code indicating container category and physical characteristics.
summary: The type code complements the size code under ISO standards. It identifies features such as open-top or refrigerated. This supports correct usage and stowage.

definition: A facility where full and empty containers are received, stored, and delivered.
summary: Container yards support FCL operations. They may also pack cargo on behalf of merchants. CYs are essential for equipment circulation.

definition: Indicating that goods have been stowed inside a container.
summary: Containerised cargo benefits from standardized handling. It improves protection and efficiency. The term distinguishes boxed cargo from break bulk.

definition: Goods forbidden by law to be imported or exported.
summary: Contraband is subject to seizure by authorities. Transporting such goods carries legal penalties. Compliance with customs laws is essential.

definition: A legally enforceable agreement defining rights and obligations between parties.
summary: Contracts govern commercial relationships. They specify duties, consideration, and remedies. In logistics, contracts define transport and service terms.

definition: The outsourcing of logistics activities under a contractual arrangement.
summary: Contract logistics covers warehousing, transport, and distribution. It allows companies to focus on core business. Service levels are defined contractually.

definition: A system integrating technical data from multiple sources under contractor management.
summary: This service supports defense and complex systems. It integrates contractor, subcontractor, and government databases. Access and maintenance are contractually defined.

definition: A designated port used for tariff and documentation purposes even if the vessel does not call there.
summary: This port equalizes inland haulage and tariffs. It is commonly shown on bills of lading. The concept simplifies commercial arrangements.

definition: The monitoring and regulation of activities and data against defined procedures.
summary: Control ensures compliance with standards. It involves checks, supervision, and corrective action. Effective control supports reliability.

definition: Cargo transported without containerization.
summary: Conventional cargo is handled piece by piece. It requires more labor than containerized cargo. It remains common for certain commodities.

definition: An auxiliary undercarriage used to convert a semitrailer into a full trailer.
summary: Converter dollies include a fifth wheel and tow bar. They improve flexibility in road transport. They are widely used in trailer operations.

definition: The act of transporting goods from one place to another.
summary: Conveyance applies to all transport modes. It includes the movement itself and the means used. The term is common in legal contexts.

definition: A mechanical system used to move goods continuously.
summary: Conveyors improve efficiency in terminals and warehouses. They reduce manual handling. Common types include belt and roller conveyors.

definition: A combination of skills and technologies that provide competitive advantage.
summary: Core competences differentiate a business. They support multiple products or services. Firms focus investment on these strengths.

definition: Structural fittings at container corners used for handling and securing.
summary: Corner fittings enable lifting, stacking, and lashing. They are standardized globally. Safe container operations depend on them.

definition: A vertical structural member connecting top and bottom corner fittings of a container.
summary: Corner posts provide strength and stability. They form part of the container frame. Damage affects container safety.

definition: A message replacing incorrect information in a prior data exchange.
summary: Correction messages ensure data accuracy. They follow agreed interchange standards. They are common in electronic documentation.

definition: Established local practices governing port operations.
summary: Customs of port influence handling and procedures. They supplement written rules. Knowledge of local custom avoids disputes.

definition: A condition where the customer arranges transport of the container to and from the terminal or depot.
summary: Under COT, the customer is responsible for inland transport movements. The container must still be returned to the agreed terminal or depot. This arrangement shifts operational responsibility to the customer.

term: Council of European and Japanese National Shipowner’s Associations
definition: An international organization representing European and Japanese shipowners.
summary: CENSA promotes sound shipping policies across all shipping sectors. It coordinates member positions and represents them in discussions with other shipowner groups. The council focuses on regulatory, commercial, and strategic shipping matters.

definition: The country from which a means of transport departs or is scheduled to depart.
summary: This term is used for transport and customs documentation. It identifies the starting point of the transport movement. It may differ from the country of origin.

definition: The country from which goods are shipped.
summary: Country of despatch refers to the physical shipping location of goods. It is used in trade and customs declarations. It may differ from the country of production.

definition: The country where goods were produced or manufactured according to customs rules.
summary: Country of origin determines duty rates and trade measures. It is defined by international customs criteria. Proper declaration is legally required.

definition: The country from which goods are sent to the importing country.
summary: This term focuses on the last shipping country rather than production. It is used in customs and statistical reporting. It may differ from origin and despatch.

definition: A contract by which a vessel is hired for cargo carriage.
summary: Charter parties define rights and obligations between shipowner and charterer. They cover freight, duration, and responsibilities. Common in bulk and tramp shipping.

definition: A condition where port dues are paid by the charterer.
summary: CPD allocates port cost responsibility to the charterer. It is specified in charter parties. This affects voyage cost calculations.

definition: An Incoterm where the seller pays carriage to a named destination.
summary: Risk transfers to the buyer when goods are handed to the first carrier. Insurance is not included. CPT can be used for all transport modes.

definition: A charter party term indicating loading or discharge at customary speed.
summary: CQD avoids fixed loading rates. Performance is measured against local norms. Disputes may arise if customs are unclear.

definition: The freight rate applicable at a given time.
summary: Current rates fluctuate with market conditions. They are used for spot pricing. Rates may vary by route and cargo.

definition: A machine designed to lift and move heavy loads using a projecting arm or beam.
summary: Cranes are essential for cargo handling in ports and terminals. They improve efficiency and safety. Types include quay, gantry, and mobile cranes.

definition: A person employed on board a vessel and listed in the crew list.
summary: Crew members perform operational and service duties. They are governed by maritime regulations. Proper certification is required.

definition: The point at which sufficient participants enable efficient market activity.
summary: Critical mass allows frequent and reliable transactions. It improves liquidity and pricing efficiency. Often discussed in digital marketplaces.

definition: A project planning technique identifying activities that determine total project duration.
summary: CPM highlights tasks that cannot be delayed. It supports scheduling and control. Widely used in logistics and construction projects.

definition: Cargo that remains on a vessel after discharge.
summary: CROB is used in port and voyage reporting. It helps reconcile cargo figures. Often applied in bulk and tanker trades.

definition: Shipping services between countries other than the vessel’s flag state.
summary: Cross trades are common in international shipping. They allow flexible deployment of vessels. Governed by international regulations.

definition: A clause allowing cargo retention due to delivery shortages.
summary: CRTs arose in response to oil cargo shortages. They protect charterers. The clause is negotiated contractually.

definition: A unit of measurement for kinematic viscosity.
summary: Centistokes are used to classify fuel oil viscosity. This affects engine performance and handling. Common in bunker specifications.

definition: A passenger vessel operating scheduled leisure voyages with tourist stops.
summary: Cruise ships focus on passenger accommodation and services. They do not normally carry cargo. Voyages include planned port visits.

definition: An indication that cargo or equipment is fitted within a container.
summary: CTR is used in operational and cargo descriptions. It confirms container compatibility. Context determines specific application.

definition: A medium of exchange defined by monetary authorities.
summary: Currencies are standardized under ISO 4217. They enable trade and settlement. Exchange rates affect international logistics costs.

definition: Cargo collected by the customer from a warehouse or facility.
summary: Customer pick up shifts responsibility to the buyer. Timing and documentation are critical. Common in domestic distribution.

definition: Activities that support and satisfy customer requirements during a commercial relationship.
summary: Customer service adds value beyond the core product. It includes communication and problem resolution. High service levels improve retention.

definition: A measure of how well customer orders are fulfilled against agreed terms.
summary: Service level reflects reliability and responsiveness. It is tracked using performance metrics. Higher levels indicate better execution.

definition: The government authority responsible for regulating imports and exports.
summary: Customs collect duties and enforce trade regulations. They control prohibited and restricted goods. Compliance is mandatory.

definition: An authorized agent handling customs clearance on behalf of traders.
summary: Customs brokers prepare and submit documentation. They ensure compliance with regulations. Their expertise speeds clearance.

definition: An invoice used by customs to determine the value of imported goods.
summary: The invoice states price, costs, and terms. It supports duty assessment. Accuracy is legally required.

definition: The monetary value declared to customs for duty and statistics.
summary: Customs value determines payable duties and taxes. It follows international valuation rules. Misdeclaration can lead to penalties.

definition: The study of control and communication in complex systems.
summary: Cybernetics applies to mechanical and information systems. It focuses on feedback and regulation. It influences logistics automation.

definition: Charges applied for container handling at the destination yard.
summary: CYC covers storage and terminal services. It is billed to cargo interests. Rates vary by port.

definition: An account used to record port-related expenses paid on behalf of a vessel or principal.
