summary: A disbursement account consolidates costs such as port dues, pilotage, towage, and agency fees incurred during a vessel’s port call. It is commonly settled between shipowners, charterers, and agents as part of voyage accounting.

definition: An obsolete Incoterm under which the seller delivered goods cleared for export at a named frontier point.
summary: DAF was removed from Incoterms after the 2010 revision and is no longer in use. It should not be used in new contracts and has been replaced by more modern Incoterms such as DAP or DDP.

definition: A written statement documenting damage found on cargo or transport equipment.
summary: This report is typically prepared by a surveyor, carrier, or terminal operator upon discovery of damage. It is used for claims handling, insurance purposes, and liability assessment.

definition: A penalty payable when cargo is not ready for loading upon vessel arrival within laycan.
summary: DAMFORDET applies only when cargo is not available at the agreed time and is distinct from detention for delayed vessel operations. If cargo is ready on arrival, no DAMFORDET is payable.

definition: Goods whose transport presents a risk to people, property, equipment, or the environment.
summary: Dangerous goods are regulated under international conventions such as the IMDG Code. Proper classification, documentation, packaging, and labeling are mandatory.

definition: A document certifying that dangerous goods are correctly described, packed, and labeled for transport.
summary: It is issued by the consignor in accordance with applicable regulations and conventions. The declaration confirms compliance with safety and transport requirements.

definition: A declaration confirming that dangerous goods have been properly packed and secured in a container.
summary: This document forms part of the dangerous goods declaration and confirms compliance with IMDG rules. It certifies the container is clean, suitable, and correctly loaded.

definition: The total number of days allowed for both loading and discharging operations.
summary: DAPS combines loading and discharge time into a single laytime allowance. It is commonly used in charter party agreements.

definition: A metal plate affixed to a container showing key identification and technical data.
summary: The data plate typically displays tare weight, gross weight, payload, dimensions, and approval references. It is essential for safety, compliance, and inspection purposes.

definition: An obsolete Incoterm under which the seller delivered goods without paying import duties or taxes.
summary: DDU was removed from Incoterms after 2010 and is no longer valid for new contracts. It should not be used and has been replaced by DAP or DDP depending on responsibility allocation.

definition: An Incoterm under which the seller delivers goods cleared for import and pays all duties and taxes.
summary: DDP places maximum responsibility on the seller, including import clearance and local charges. It remains a valid Incoterm and can be used for any mode of transport.

definition: The difference between the actual and calculated draft of a vessel.
summary: Deadload may arise due to measurement inaccuracies, water density variations, or loading discrepancies. It is monitored during stability and loading assessments.

definition: The maximum total weight a vessel can safely carry at its maximum permitted draft.
summary: Deadweight includes cargo, fuel, water, provisions, stores, and spare parts. It represents the difference between lightship weight and loaded displacement.

definition: A computer-based system that supports decision-making by generating alternative solutions.
summary: DSS is used for complex or unstructured problems where managerial judgment is required. It enhances planning, analysis, and control functions.

definition: A permanent horizontal structure covering part of a vessel’s hull or compartments.
summary: Decks provide structural strength and working surfaces for cargo, crew, and equipment. Multiple deck levels may exist depending on vessel design.

definition: A statement certifying the origin of goods for customs and trade purposes.
summary: It is made by the manufacturer, exporter, or authorized party. The declaration supports tariff treatment, trade restrictions, and compliance requirements.

definition: The value of goods declared by the shipper to establish carrier liability or charges.

definition: Inventory held to allow independent control of successive operations.
summary: Decoupling inventory absorbs variability between processes with differing rates. It improves flexibility and operational stability.

definition: The point in the supply chain where inventory buffers different input and output rates.

definition: A vessel tank designed for the carriage of liquid bulk cargoes such as vegetable oils.

definition: A standard charge applied when no specific rate is defined.
summary: Default charges apply in the absence of agreed or published tariffs. They provide a fallback pricing mechanism.

definition: The process of splitting consolidated shipments into individual consignments.
summary: Degroupage typically occurs at destination terminals or warehouses. It facilitates final delivery to multiple consignees.

definition: An obsolete Incoterm under which goods were delivered on the quay at the destination port.
summary: DEQ was removed from Incoterms after 2010 and should not be used in new contracts. It has been functionally replaced by DAP or DDP depending on cost and risk allocation.

definition: A lifting device on board a vessel consisting of a vertical post and an inclined spar used for cargo handling.

definition: An obsolete Incoterm under which the seller delivered goods on board the vessel at the destination port.
summary: DES was removed from Incoterms after 2010 and should not be used in new contracts. It has been replaced by DAP or DDP depending on delivery responsibilities.

definition: A reward payable to charterers when loading or discharging is completed in less time than allowed.

definition: A document or message informing the consignee that goods have been sent or are ready for shipment.

definition: The number of days saved when allowed free time for equipment or operations is not fully used.
summary: Despatch days form the basis for calculating despatch money. They reflect operational efficiency during cargo handling.

definition: The final place to which goods or a vehicle are contractually bound.
summary: Destination is defined in the contract of carriage. It determines routing, delivery obligations, and liability endpoints.

definition: The retention of transport equipment beyond the agreed free time period.

definition: The reduction in quality or condition of goods due to time, damage, or external influences.

definition: A Norwegian classification society providing ship classification and technical assurance services.

definition: A vessel’s departure from the agreed or customary voyage route.

definition: Freight payable for cargo space booked but not utilized.

definition: The measurements of cargo expressed as length, width, and height.

definition: The transfer of leased equipment from one lessee to another.

definition: The shortest operational route between two points.

definition: Expenses paid by a ship’s agent on behalf of the carrier at a port.

definition: The unloading of cargo from a vessel, vehicle, or aircraft.

definition: A difference between declared information and actual findings.

definition: The elimination of traditional intermediaries through direct buyer-seller interaction.

summary: Outsiders compete with conference carriers on the same trade lanes. They are not bound by conference tariffs or agreements.

definition: Administrative and physical operations applied to goods leaving a production or storage facility.
summary: Outward handling covers activities from order execution to departure. It includes documentation, packing, staging, and loading.

definition: Over the side of a vessel or out of the ship.
summary: The term is used to describe objects or substances falling or being discharged into the sea. It may carry safety or environmental implications.

definition: Carrier in a consortium carrying cargo beyond its allocated share.
summary: Overcarriage occurs when a member exceeds agreed allotments. It may require compensation or adjustment among consortium partners.

definition: Comprehensive inspection and repair of equipment or systems.
summary: Overhauls restore functionality and extend service life. They are typically scheduled based on usage, time, or regulatory requirements.

definition: Cargo exceeding standard height limits.
summary: Overheight cargo often requires open top containers or flat racks. Special permits and handling procedures are usually necessary.

definition: Cargo exceeding standard length limits.
summary: Overlength cargo may extend beyond container frames or transport units. It requires route planning and specialized equipment.

definition: A unit containing one or more packages combined for handling and stowage convenience.
summary: Overpacks are commonly used for dangerous goods shipments. All marking, labeling, and regulatory requirements must remain visible and compliant.

definition: Work performed beyond normal working hours, usually paid at a premium rate.
summary: Overtime is common in port, terminal, and logistics operations. It affects labor costs and operational planning.

definition: Cargo exceeding standard width limits.
summary: Overwidth cargo often requires special stowage positions and transport permits. Safety clearances and escort requirements may apply.

definition: The legal owner of cargo, equipment, or means of transport.
summary: Ownership determines rights, liabilities, and insurance interests. It may differ from the operator or user of the asset.

definition: Prefix identifying the registered owner of a container.
summary: The code is part of the container identification number. It is used for tracking, control, and regulatory purposes.

definition: Trucker who owns and operates their own vehicle.
summary: Owner-operators are independent carriers in road transport. They often contract directly with shippers or logistics providers.

definition: Collective term referring to the owners of a vessel or asset.
summary: Owners hold legal title and ultimate responsibility. In shipping, they are distinct from charterers and operators.

definition: Mutual marine insurance covering third-party liabilities arising from vessel operations.
summary: P&I insurance covers risks not included in hull and machinery policies, such as cargo damage, pollution, crew claims, and collision liabilities. It is typically provided by P&I Clubs operating on a mutual, non-profit basis for shipowners and operators.

definition: The physical preparation of goods and their containment to facilitate handling and transport.
summary: Packing refers both to the act of enclosing goods and the final packed unit itself. Proper packing protects cargo, supports efficient handling, and reduces the risk of damage during transport.

definition: Materials and processes used to contain, protect, and present goods for transport and storage.
summary: Packaging includes boxes, crates, drums, and other materials designed to safeguard cargo. It plays a critical role in cargo integrity, compliance, and supply-chain efficiency.

definition: An internal document specifying how goods must be packed.
summary: Packing instructions standardize packing methods to ensure safety, compliance, and efficiency. They are commonly used in manufacturing and logistics environments.

definition: A document detailing the contents of each individual package in a shipment.
summary: The packing list supports customs clearance, cargo verification, and handling operations. It complements, but does not replace, commercial invoices and transport documents.

definition: A flat platform used to stack goods for handling by forklifts or slings.
summary: Pallets enable efficient cargo handling, storage, and transport. They are standardized to support intermodal logistics operations.

definition: The maximum vessel dimensions permitted to transit the Panama Canal.
summary: Panamax standards influence vessel design and global trade routes. They serve as an important benchmark in fleet planning and chartering.

definition: A partial loss borne solely by the owner of the damaged property.
summary: Particular average differs from general average in that losses are not shared. It applies to cargo or vessel damage caused by insured perils affecting only one interest.

definition: The location where a shipment is delivered to the consignee.
summary: The place of delivery marks the end of the carrier’s transport liability. It is a critical term in contracts of carriage and Incoterms.

definition: The location where the carrier receives goods from the shipper.
summary: This point defines when the carrier’s responsibility for the cargo begins. It is frequently used in multimodal transport documents.

definition: The revenue-producing cargo carried by a transport unit.
summary: Payload excludes tare weight and consumables. Maximizing payload efficiency is essential for transport economics.

definition: A payment arrangement where documents are released only upon payment.
summary: This method reduces seller risk by ensuring payment before cargo release. It is commonly used in international trade banking.

definition: The process of selecting goods from inventory to fulfill orders.
summary: Picking accuracy directly affects customer satisfaction and warehouse efficiency. It is often supported by picking lists or digital systems.

definition: Goods that are in transit between origin and destination.
summary: Pipeline inventory ties up working capital while goods move through the supply chain. Effective planning minimizes delays and excess stock exposure.

definition: The location where a carrier receives a consignment from the shipper and where the carrier’s liability for the transport begins.
summary: Place of Acceptance defines the contractual starting point of the carrier’s responsibility in a transport chain. It is commonly used in transport documents, multimodal contracts, and liability determinations. The term is synonymous with Place of Receipt in most commercial contexts.

definition: The location where a consignment is delivered to the consignee and where the carrier’s liability for the transport ends.
summary: Place of Delivery marks the contractual endpoint of the carrier’s transport responsibility. It is critical for determining risk transfer, claims handling, and contract performance. This term is widely used in bills of lading and multimodal transport agreements.

definition: The location where a carrier takes charge of goods from the shipper at the start of the transport venture.
summary: Place of Receipt establishes when and where carrier liability commences. It is functionally equivalent to Place of Acceptance and is frequently referenced in combined transport documents. The term is especially relevant in door-to-door and intermodal movements.

definition: The activity of positioning goods or objects in a selected location or position.
summary: Placement refers to the physical act of locating cargo, equipment, or assets within a facility or transport unit. It plays a role in warehouse operations, stowage planning, and production layouts. Proper placement supports efficiency, safety, and accessibility.

definition: The process of setting objectives over a defined period and determining how to achieve them using available resources.
summary: Planning provides structure and direction to operational and strategic activities. In logistics and supply chain management, it supports capacity allocation, scheduling, and cost control. Effective planning aligns resources with demand and organizational goals.

definition: The time period covered by a specific plan.
summary: Planning Horizon defines how far into the future decisions are considered. Short horizons focus on execution, while longer horizons address strategy and investment. The concept is widely used in production planning, forecasting, and supply chain design.

definition: A container consisting only of a reinforced floor, designed for the carriage of heavy or uncontainerable cargo.
summary: Container platforms are used for oversized or heavy cargo that cannot fit into standard container types. Multiple platforms may be combined to create a larger base. They are commonly employed in project cargo and heavy-lift logistics.

definition: The area at an airport where aircraft are parked for loading, unloading, and embarkation.
summary: In air cargo operations, the platform serves as the interface between aircraft and ground handling activities. It supports cargo transfer, servicing, and staging. The term is synonymous with apron or ramp in aviation contexts.

definition: A truck or trailer body consisting only of a floor, without sides, ends, or roof.
summary: Platform bodies are designed for transporting oversized or irregular cargo. They allow unrestricted loading from all sides and are common in heavy haulage and project logistics. Securement is achieved through lashing and blocking rather than enclosure.

definition: A line marked on a ship’s hull indicating the maximum safe loading level under various conditions.
summary: The Plimsoll Mark ensures vessels are not overloaded beyond safe limits. Its position varies with water density and seasonal regulations. It is a fundamental safety and regulatory feature in merchant shipping.

definition: A relative value assigned to an empty container at a specific depot location to quantify imbalance costs.
summary: Point Values are used in container management systems to calculate credits or charges for empty repositioning. They are derived from forecasted flows, repositioning costs, and storage expenses. The mechanism supports efficient container fleet optimization.

definition: A flat-deck vessel with shallow draft.
summary: Pontoons are used for construction, temporary bridging, and transport in shallow waters. Their flat structure allows flexible loading and operational versatility. They are common in ports, rivers, and offshore projects.

definition: The shared use of equipment or assets by multiple companies through joint investment or agreement.
summary: Pooling arrangements reduce capital expenditure and improve asset utilization. They are common for containers, chassis, and transport equipment. Pooling requires clear governance and allocation rules to function effectively.

definition: The aft part of a vessel where the steering engine is located.
summary: The poop is traditionally associated with navigational and steering functions. It forms part of the vessel’s superstructure at the stern. The term is rooted in nautical architecture and seamanship.

definition: A harbor equipped with facilities for vessels to berth, load, and discharge cargo.
summary: Ports function as critical nodes in global trade and transport networks. They support cargo handling, storage, customs, and intermodal connections. The term may also denote the left side of a vessel when facing forward.

definition: A port where a vessel stops during a voyage to berth or anchor.
summary: Ports of Call are listed in voyage schedules and charter agreements. They determine routing, transit time, and commercial obligations. A vessel may have multiple ports of call on a single voyage.

definition: The port where cargo is unloaded from a sea-going vessel.
summary: Port of Discharge defines where the maritime leg of transport ends. It is a key reference point for delivery obligations and onward transport planning. The term is standard in bills of lading and charter parties.

definition: The port where cargo is loaded onto a sea-going vessel.
summary: Port of Loading marks the commencement of the ocean transport leg. It is used for freight calculation, risk allocation, and documentation. Accurate designation is essential for contractual clarity.

definition: A gantry crane with vertical legs allowing vehicles or rail equipment to pass underneath.
summary: Portal cranes are widely used in ports and terminals for heavy lifting operations. Their design supports efficient cargo transfer across transport modes. They are essential for container, bulk, and project cargo handling.

definition: A statement recording a vessel’s port call details such as arrival, departure, drafts, and cargo operations.
summary: Portlogs provide an operational record of a vessel’s activities at a port. They are used for performance analysis, claims, and voyage accounting. The document captures both technical and commercial particulars.

definition: An MRO-focused procurement marketplace for routine, non-core business purchases such as office supplies, travel services, or IT equipment.
summary: Procurement hubs support indirect purchasing and are typically horizontal markets rather than industry-specific. They aggregate suppliers and standardize buying processes to reduce transaction costs and improve efficiency.

definition: The control and management of material flows up to the manufacturing or production process.
summary: Procurement logistics ensures that inputs arrive in the correct quantity, quality, place, and time. It directly supports production continuity and inventory optimization.

definition: The result or output of a process, including goods or services produced.
summary: A product represents the end item delivered to a customer or market. In logistics and manufacturing, it is the focal point around which supply chains are designed.

definition: All phases involved in the transformation or production process of a product.
summary: The product chain traces value creation from raw materials through processing and assembly. It is often analyzed to identify efficiency improvements and cost drivers.

definition: The time period from a product’s market introduction to its withdrawal from the market.
summary: The product life cycle includes introduction, growth, maturity, saturation, decline, and end phases. Logistics strategies often adapt to each phase to balance cost and service.

definition: The conversion of materials or assembly of components into goods, products, or services.
summary: Production may be measured in physical or financial terms over a defined period. It forms the core activity linking procurement, logistics, and distribution.

definition: A relative measure of output per unit of input such as labor hours or machine hours.
summary: Productivity is a key performance indicator in operations and logistics. Improvements typically result from process optimization or technology adoption.

definition: An organizational unit held accountable for its own revenues, costs, and profits.
summary: Profit centres support decentralized management and financial accountability. They are commonly used in large logistics and transport organizations.

definition: A document or receipt signed by the consignee confirming delivery of goods.
summary: Proof of Delivery is used to confirm contractual fulfillment and trigger invoicing or payment. It is critical for dispute resolution and claims handling.

definition: The prescribed name used to describe goods on shipping documents and notifications.
summary: Proper Shipping Names are especially important for dangerous goods compliance. They ensure consistent identification across regulatory and transport documentation.

definition: A standard endorsed by industry or government but not formally approved by an accredited standards body.
summary: Proprietary standards may achieve wide acceptance despite lacking formal certification. They often precede or influence official international standards.

definition: A mutual association of shipowners providing insurance coverage against third-party liabilities.
summary: P&I Clubs cover risks such as cargo damage, pollution, and crew claims. They operate on a mutual contribution basis rather than commercial premiums.

definition: A formal written record drawn up to attest specific events or agreements.
summary: Protocols are used to document inspections, incidents, or contractual milestones. They provide evidentiary support in legal and operational contexts.

definition: Government agencies or officials responsible for enforcing laws and regulations.
summary: Public authorities oversee customs, safety, security, and regulatory compliance. Their involvement is integral to international transport and trade.

definition: A warehouse offering storage and related services to multiple customers.
summary: Public warehouses provide flexible capacity without long-term commitment. They are widely used in distribution and seasonal inventory management.

definition: A distribution system where replenishment occurs based on actual demand requests.
summary: Pull systems reduce excess inventory by responding to real consumption signals. They contrast with push systems driven by forecasts.

definition: A formal order issued by a buyer to a supplier specifying goods, quantities, prices, and delivery terms.
summary: Purchase Orders establish contractual obligations between buyer and seller. They are central to procurement, invoicing, and audit control.

definition: A buyer-centric platform that aggregates demand to negotiate improved purchasing terms with suppliers.
summary: Purchasing hubs may be horizontal or vertical and support both spot and systematic buying. They leverage scale to reduce costs and improve sourcing efficiency.

definition: A commercial abbreviation indicating inclusion of an additional party or entity.
summary: PUS is used informally in contractual or commercial references to denote participation beyond the primary named parties.

definition: A distribution system in which warehouses are replenished based on supplier decisions rather than actual demand.
summary: Push distribution relies on forecasts and production planning to determine stock levels. It is commonly associated with higher inventory levels compared to pull-based systems.

definition: A charter party time unit that counts only days when weather permits cargo operations.
summary: PWWD excludes time lost due to adverse weather conditions. It is frequently used in voyage charters to calculate laytime fairly.

definition: A coded data element that provides specific meaning to another data element or segment.
summary: Qualifiers are widely used in EDI and structured data exchanges. They ensure accurate interpretation of standardized messages.

definition: The totality of features and characteristics of a product or service that determine its ability to satisfy stated or implied needs.
summary: Quality is defined under ISO 8402 and forms the basis of the ISO 9000 family of standards. It applies equally to physical goods and services.

definition: Planned and systematic actions implemented to provide confidence that quality requirements will be met.
summary: Quality assurance focuses on process design and prevention rather than inspection. It is a core element of ISO-based management systems.

definition: Operational techniques and activities used to fulfill quality requirements.
summary: Quality control emphasizes inspection, testing, and corrective actions. It operates at the execution level of production or service delivery.

definition: A reduced unit rate applied to shipments that meet specific minimum quantity thresholds.
summary: Quantity charges are commonly used in air cargo tariffs. They incentivize shippers to consolidate larger volumes.

definition: A proportional reduction in rates based on the quantity shipped.
summary: Quantity discounts reward higher shipment volumes. They are a standard pricing mechanism in transport and logistics contracts.

definition: The isolation of a vessel, cargo, crew, or passengers suspected of carrying contagious disease.
summary: Quarantine measures are imposed by public authorities to prevent disease spread. They can significantly affect port operations and schedules.

definition: A structure along the waterfront предназнач for the mooring of vessels.
summary: Quays provide access for loading and discharging cargo. The term is often used interchangeably with pier in port terminology.

definition: An ordered collection of data or tasks waiting to be processed sequentially.
summary: Queues are fundamental in computer systems and logistics planning. They ensure first-in, first-out processing discipline.

definition: A timber wedge used to secure drums or cargo against movement.
summary: Quoins are commonly applied in breakbulk and project cargo stowage. They enhance cargo stability during transport.

definition: Controls that limit the quantity of goods produced, imported, or exported.
summary: Quotas are trade regulation instruments used by governments. They directly affect supply volumes and market access.

definition: A stated price for specified services or goods under defined conditions.
summary: Quotations are typically time-bound and subject to conditions of carriage. They form the commercial basis for transport agreements.

definition: The date after which a quoted price is no longer valid.
summary: Quotation expiration dates protect suppliers from cost fluctuations. New rates must be issued once validity lapses.

definition: Trade restraints that limit the volume of goods allowed into or out of a country.
summary: Quota restrictions were largely abolished within the EC by 1968. Many have also been removed under international trade agreements.

definition: A wheeled wagon designed for the transport of cargo by rail.
summary: Rail cars are used in inland freight transport to move bulk, containerized, and general cargo over rail networks. They form a core component of intermodal logistics chains linking ports, terminals, and inland destinations.

definition: A document evidencing a contract for the transport of goods by rail.
summary: The rail consignment note serves as proof of carriage and contains details of the shipper, consignee, cargo, and routing. It is used for operational control, claims handling, and regulatory compliance in rail transport.

definition: An artificial inclined path that allows wheeled vehicles, cargo, or trailers to change elevation during loading or unloading.
summary: Ramps are commonly used in Roll-on/Roll-off vessel operations and terminal facilities. They enable efficient movement of cargo units without lifting equipment.

definition: The price charged for a transport service or the measured amount applied in pricing.
summary: Rates form the basis of freight cost calculation and may vary by quantity, distance, mode, or service level. They are typically governed by tariffs, contracts, or spot market conditions.

definition: A factor used to calculate a monetary amount or charge.
summary: Rates of calculation are applied in freight, storage, or handling charges where costs depend on weight, volume, or time. They ensure standardized and transparent cost computation.

definition: The party to whom a shipment is consigned and delivered.
summary: The receiver is responsible for accepting delivery and may be liable for charges depending on contractual terms. Accurate identification of the receiver is essential for successful cargo.

definition: A recapitulation of agreed terms and conditions.
summary: Recaps are commonly used in chartering and freight negotiations to confirm commercial agreements. They provide a concise summary prior to contract finalization.

definition: A written acknowledgment confirming that goods or documents have been received.
summary: Receipts serve as proof of delivery or handover in logistics transactions. They are often required for claims, audits, and payment verification.

definition: The figure indicating the speed at which a means of transport changes course, expressed in degrees per minute.
summary: Rate of turn is a navigational parameter used primarily for vessels and aircraft. It is important for safe maneuvering, collision avoidance, and compliance with navigational standards.

definition: A class to which an article is assigned for transport or tariff purposes.
summary: Ratings are used to determine applicable rates, handling requirements, and regulatory treatment. They are common in tariff systems, especially in air and surface cargo pricing.

definition: An operating system capability that responds to external events within a short and predictable time frame.
summary: Real-time systems support continuous operational processes rather than batch processing. They are widely used in logistics tracking, automation, and control systems.

definition: That part of a transport charge which the carrier agrees to return.
summary: Rebates may arise from commercial agreements, service issues, or overcharges. They are subject to contractual and tariff conditions.

definition: A recapitulation of the terms and conditions agreed.
summary: Recaps are commonly used in chartering and freight negotiations to summarize agreed commercial terms. They often precede formal contract documentation.

definition: A written acknowledgement that something has been received.
summary: Receipts provide proof of delivery or handover of goods or documents. They are important for claims handling, audits, and payment verification.

definition: The carrier that receives a consignment on behalf of another carrier, agent, or shipper for onward transport.
summary: Receiving carriers initiate the transport chain in interline or multimodal movements. They are responsible for initial cargo acceptance and documentation accuracy.

definition: Goods that have arrived at a receiving location but are not yet available for use or sale.
summary: Receiving stock represents inventory awaiting inspection, verification, or system entry. It is a transitional stage in warehouse operations.

definition: Activities connected with restoring or adjusting the packaging of a product.
summary: Reconditioning ensures goods are presented in acceptable condition after transport. It is common in retail, fashion, and consumer goods logistics.

definition: The process of restoring garments to shop-ready condition after transport.
summary: This process may include steaming, pressing, or repackaging. It is commonly used in fashion logistics and retail distribution.

definition: The return of a shipment to the party that originally delivered it, or the return of a chartered vessel to its owner.
summary: Redelivery occurs at contract completion or due to refusal or error. Conditions are defined in transport contracts or charter parties.

definition: A refrigerated transport unit with insulated walls and a self-powered cooling system.
summary: Reefers are primarily used for food and other temperature-sensitive cargo. They maintain controlled conditions throughout transit.

definition: Cargo that requires temperature control during transport.
summary: Reefer cargo includes perishables and pharmaceuticals. Strict temperature management is essential to preserve quality and safety.

definition: A thermal container fitted with mechanical or absorption refrigeration equipment.
summary: Reefer containers are used in maritime and intermodal transport. They enable precise temperature control across the supply chain.

definition: Charges for subsequent surface or air transport arranged by a forwarder but not covered under the Air Waybill.
summary: Reforwarding charges apply after arrival at the destination airport. They are payable by the forwarder or consignee rather than the air carrier.

definition: The repayment of all or part of a transport charge for unused carriage.
summary: Refunds arise from cancellations, overpayments, or unused services. They are governed by carrier tariffs and contractual terms.

definition: A specified geographical area defined for operational purposes.
summary: Regions are used for planning, pricing, and regulatory application. They help standardize transport and logistics operations.

definition: The process of splitting consignments and combining them into new shipments.
summary: Regroupage improves transport efficiency by consolidating smaller shipments. It is widely used in freight forwarding and distribution networks.

definition: A procedure in which goods shipped directly from supplier to customer are invoiced first to an intermediary and subsequently by the intermediary to the final customer.
summary: Re-invoicing is commonly used in international trade structures involving traders or intermediaries. It allows commercial control, margin management, and compliance with contractual or fiscal arrangements.

definition: The non-acceptance of cargo or goods by the receiving party.
summary: Rejection may occur due to damage, non-compliance with specifications, or documentation issues. It often triggers returns, claims, or dispute resolution processes.

definition: A practice in the less-than-truckload industry where drivers sequentially operate the same truck in shifts.
summary: Relay operations maximize vehicle utilization and reduce transit time. The method resembles a relay or pony express system common in long-haul trucking.

definition: The consistency of a supplier in meeting agreed delivery terms.
summary: Delivery reliability covers adherence to quality, quantity, timing, conditions, and pricing. It is a key performance indicator in supply chain management.

definition: An interchangeable subject differing physically from the original and requiring additional machining or provisions for installation.
summary: Replacements are functionally equivalent but may need adaptation. This distinction is important for maintenance, engineering, and spare-parts logistics.

definition: The completion or refilling of stock levels.
summary: Replenishment ensures inventory availability to meet demand. It may be driven by forecasts, reorder points, or pull-based systems.

definition: An invitation to suppliers to submit bids for complex products or services.
summary: RFPs are used when requirements cannot be fully predefined. They evaluate both technical solutions and commercial terms.

definition: An invitation to suppliers to quote prices for clearly defined products or services.
summary: RFQs focus primarily on price and delivery terms. They are commonly used for standardized or repeat purchases.

definition: Advance allotment of space or weight capacity for transport.
summary: Reservations secure transport capacity ahead of shipment. They are critical in peak seasons and capacity-constrained markets.

definition: The carrier legally liable for the transport of goods as stated in the transport document.
summary: In consortium or interline transport, the responsible carrier bears contractual liability. The role is defined in bills of lading or air waybills.

definition: Goods sent back to their original place of acceptance.
summary: Returns may result from rejection, warranty issues, or commercial agreements. Reverse logistics processes typically manage returned goods.

definition: Income generated from the provision of transport services.
summary: Revenue is derived from freight rates, surcharges, and ancillary services. It forms the financial basis of carrier operations.

definition: A procurement method where buyers post demand and suppliers compete by bidding prices downward.
summary: Reverse actions leverage buyer power to reduce costs. They are widely used in electronic marketplaces and strategic sourcing platforms.

definition: The collection of used, damaged, or obsolete products and packaging from end-users.
summary: Reverse distribution supports recycling, disposal, and refurbishment. It is a core component of sustainable supply chain practices.

definition: A certificate issued by the Italian authorities permitting the carriage of dangerous goods in Italian waters.
summary: The RINA certificate confirms regulatory compliance for hazardous cargo. It is mandatory for certain vessel operations in Italy.

definition: A party undertaking the transport of goods by road under a transport contract.
summary: Road carriers provide domestic and international haulage services. They operate trucks and manage driver, vehicle, and compliance obligations.

definition: A semitrailer designed to operate both on highways and railway tracks.
summary: Road railers enable seamless intermodal transport without cargo transshipment. They are commonly associated with specialized rail systems.

definition: A means of transport authorized to operate on public roads.
summary: Road vehicles include trucks, trailers, and tractors used in freight transport. Their use is subject to traffic and safety regulations.

definition: Cargo, fuel, or stores that remain on board a vessel after discharge.
summary: ROB is commonly referenced in bunker accounting and cargo documentation. It affects voyage calculations and operational planning.

definition: A specialized trailer used for terminal haulage and stowage on roll-on roll-off vessels.
summary: Roll trailers facilitate efficient RoRo operations. They are designed for heavy and oversized cargo handling.

definition: The frictional force generated between vehicle tyres and the road surface.
summary: Rolling resistance affects fuel consumption and vehicle efficiency. It is a key consideration in vehicle and tyre design.

definition: A vessel loading system where cargo is driven on and off using ramps.
summary: RoRo systems enable fast loading of vehicles and trailers. They are widely used in short-sea shipping and ferry services.

definition: The sequence of ports visited by a vessel during a voyage.
summary: Rotation planning impacts transit times and service reliability. It is a core element of liner shipping schedules.

definition: A journey from an origin to a destination and back again.
summary: Round trips are used in voyage planning and cost calculations. They influence asset utilization and scheduling efficiency.

definition: The path along which goods are transported.
summary: Routes are selected based on cost, time, safety, and regulatory factors. They apply across all transport modes.

definition: The process of determining the most efficient transport route for a shipment.
summary: Routing supports cost optimization, timely delivery, and navigational safety. It may include weather routing for vessels.

definition: A vertical division of a vessel used to indicate container stowage positions.
summary: Rows are numbered from the vessel centerline outward. They are essential for precise stowage planning and documentation.

definition: A freight calculation unit equal to one metric tonne or one cubic meter, whichever is greater.
summary: Revenue tonnes determine freight charges based on weight or volume. The total RT is multiplied by the applicable freight rate.

definition: A standardized customs document used for declaring goods to customs authorities.
summary: The Single Administrative Document simplifies and harmonizes customs procedures within certain customs regimes. It is widely used for import, export, and transit declarations.

definition: The maximum load that a lifting appliance is permitted to handle safely.
summary: Safe Working Load is determined by design, testing, and regulatory standards. Exceeding SWL poses serious safety and liability risks.

definition: Inventory held to protect against uncertainty in demand or supply.
summary: Safety stock mitigates risks from forecast errors, lead-time variability, and supply disruptions. In production planning it may also represent planned overcapacity or overplanning.

definition: A bill of lading term indicating the carrier relies on the shipper’s description of cargo contents.
summary: STC limits the carrier’s responsibility for cargo description accuracy. It is commonly used for sealed units such as containers or cartons.

definition: The rescue or recovery of a vessel and/or cargo from danger at sea.
summary: Salvage operations aim to prevent loss or damage and may give rise to salvage awards. They are governed by maritime law and international conventions.

definition: A time reference indicating Saturday afternoon or evening.
summary: SATPM is commonly used in chartering, port operations, and laytime calculations. It clarifies time-related contractual obligations.

definition: A berth that can be safely reached, used, and left by a vessel.
summary: A safe berth must be free from hazards under normal conditions. The obligation is often defined in charter party clauses.

definition: A freight measurement unit used in certain commodity trades.
summary: Scale tons vary by trade and commodity. They are applied according to agreed tariff or charter terms.

definition: A planned timetable for vessel, transport, or operational activities.
summary: Schedules define arrival and departure times and port sequences. They are essential for coordination across transport modes.

definition: A customs procedure allowing export with minimal information by approved parties.
summary: SCP facilitates faster export processing. Full statistical and customs data are provided after shipment within a defined timeframe.

definition: A vehicle or unit having a single cargo deck.
summary: Single deckers are used where height or handling constraints apply. The term appears in road transport and equipment descriptions.

definition: Charges for transporting goods by sea only.
summary: Seafreight excludes inland haulage and terminal handling. It represents the core ocean transport cost component.

definition: A locking device used to secure containers or transport units during transit.
summary: Seals provide evidence of tampering or unauthorized access. Seal integrity is critical for customs and security compliance.

definition: A document recording seal numbers applied to cargo units.
summary: Seal logs support traceability and security audits. They are often required for customs and internal controls.

definition: Inventory accumulated in anticipation of seasonal demand peaks.
summary: Seasonal inventory smooths production and supply fluctuations. It is common in retail, agriculture, and consumer goods sectors.

definition: The condition of a vessel being fit for its intended voyage and cargo.
summary: Seaworthiness requires valid certificates, proper equipment, and competent crew. It is a fundamental obligation under maritime contracts.

definition: An airfreight rate applicable to a portion of a through route.
summary: Sectional rates apply when cargo moves over multiple route segments. They are established by scheduled air carriers.

definition: Required separation distance between incompatible cargoes.
summary: Segregation rules are defined by IMDG and BC Codes. They prevent dangerous interactions during transport.

definition: A vessel or unit capable of unloading cargo without external equipment.
summary: Self-discharging capability reduces port dependency. It is common in bulk and specialized vessels.

definition: A market condition where supply is limited and sellers hold pricing power.
summary: In a seller’s market, demand exceeds supply, leading to higher prices. Buyers have reduced negotiating leverage.

definition: A non-powered trailer designed to be towed by a tractor unit.
summary: Semi trailers transfer part of their load weight to the tractor. They are standard in road freight transport.

definition: A flatbed road trailer typically measuring around 12 meters in length.
summary: Flatbed semi trailers are used for oversized or irregular cargo. They allow flexible loading and securing.

definition: The party that consigns goods for transport.
summary: The sender is responsible for cargo description and initial delivery to the carrier. The term is synonymous with shipper.

definition: The degree to which customer orders are fulfilled under normal market conditions.
summary: Service level measures reliability and responsiveness. It is a key indicator in logistics and supply chain performance.

definition: A Service Bill is an internal documentary instrument issued between carriers or agents for control and reference purposes, not constituting a contract of carriage.
summary: A Service Bill, often referred to as a Memo Bill, is used within carrier consortia or agency networks to document shipment particulars linked to an original transport document. It records carrier names, document numbers, cargo details, and special cargo requirements but deliberately excludes freight and contractual terms. Its function is administrative traceability rather than legal carriage.

definition: An indicated temperature on transport documents specifying the air supply temperature for a container during carriage.
summary: This term is primarily used in refrigerated transport documentation to define the air delivery temperature setting. Only the temperature value itself is permitted on the Bill of Lading, excluding references to pulp or return air temperatures. It serves as an operational instruction rather than a performance guarantee.

definition: A facility used for the storage and handling of cargo prior to loading or after discharge.
summary: In port and terminal operations, a shed functions as a transitional storage area between sea and land transport. It supports consolidation, deconsolidation, and customs-related activities. Operational responsibility typically lies with terminal operators or port authorities.

definition: The defined period during which a product remains suitable for use under specified storage conditions.
summary: Shelf life is particularly relevant for perishable, chemical, and pharmaceutical goods. It establishes handling priorities and inventory rotation rules such as FIFO or FEFO. Exceeding shelf life may result in quality degradation or regulatory non-compliance.

definition: A designated segment of working time within a stevedoring or terminal operation schedule.
summary: Shifts structure labor availability across a 24-hour operational day, commonly divided into up to three shifts. They directly affect berth productivity, laytime calculations, and port cost structures. Shift definitions are often embedded in terminal tariffs and labor agreements.

definition: A charter party term indicating that Sundays and holidays are counted as working time.
summary: SHINC applies to laytime and demurrage calculations, allowing cargo operations to proceed without time exclusion. It generally benefits charterers by reducing non-working time. The term must be clearly agreed to avoid disputes.

definition: A charter party condition excluding Sundays and holidays from laytime calculations.
summary: Under SHEX terms, time lost on Sundays and holidays does not count toward laytime. This provision typically favors shipowners by extending allowable operational time. Variants such as SHEX EIU may further modify its application.

definition: An intermediary facilitating commercial arrangements between shipowners and cargo interests.
summary: Ship brokers operate in chartering, sale and purchase, and forwarding contexts. Their role includes negotiating freight rates, charter terms, and contractual conditions. They act as market specialists rather than principals to the transaction.

definition: A formal declaration made by a vessel’s master regarding extraordinary events during a voyage.
summary: A Ship’s Protest is typically lodged before a notary or competent authority upon arrival at port. It documents incidents such as heavy weather or accidents to protect the carrier from liability claims. It is often supported by logbook entries and survey reports.

definition: A distinct and identifiable quantity of goods tendered for transport.
summary: A shipment may consist of one or multiple packages moved under a single transport document. In U.S. usage, the term shipment is commonly used in place of consignment. It serves as the basic unit for tracking, documentation, and liability.

definition: The party responsible for the commercial and/or technical management of a vessel.
summary: A ship operator may be the owner or a contracted management company. Responsibilities include crewing, maintenance, compliance, and voyage execution. The operator is distinct from the charterer unless operating under bareboat terms.

definition: The legal entity registered as the owner of a vessel in the official registry.
summary: The Ship Owner’s details are recorded in the certificate of registry, including ownership shares and vessel particulars. Ownership carries ultimate responsibility for regulatory compliance and asset risk. Operational control may be delegated but ownership remains legally defined.

definition: The party by whom, in whose name, or on whose behalf a contract of carriage is concluded with a carrier.
summary: The shipper is legally responsible for tendering the goods to the carrier and for the accuracy of shipping information provided. The shipper may act directly or through an agent and is a principal party in transport documentation such as bills of lading and air waybills.

definition: A United States customs form required for certain exports to support the compilation of export statistics.
summary: The SED is completed by the shipper or authorized agent and provides details on the exporter, consignee, commodity, value, and destination. It supports trade compliance, statistical reporting, and export control enforcement.

definition: A document issued by the shipper or its agent providing instructions for document preparation and cargo forwarding.
summary: The SLI guides freight forwarders or carriers on how to prepare transport and customs documents. It typically includes routing, billing, cargo description, and special handling requirements, particularly in air cargo.

definition: A standardized, reusable transport unit designed for intermodal movement of cargo.
summary: Shipping containers conform to ISO standards and are typically 20 or 40 feet in length. They enable efficient transfer between ship, rail, and road while protecting cargo and reducing handling costs.

definition: The unloaded weight of a truck including standard equipment but excluding fuel and coolant.
summary: Shipping weight is used for regulatory, engineering, and operational calculations. It forms the basis for determining payload capacity and compliance with axle and gross vehicle weight limits.

definition: Documents required to evidence and support the carriage of goods.
summary: Shipping documents include bills of lading, waybills, packing lists, and customs forms. They serve legal, operational, and commercial purposes throughout the transport chain.

definition: A document detailing cargo particulars and the exporter’s requirements for transport.
summary: Shipping instructions are provided to carriers or forwarders to ensure correct booking, documentation, and handling. They act as the operational basis for issuing transport documents.

definition: A label affixed to a shipping unit containing identification and handling data.
summary: Shipping labels support routing, identification, and tracking of cargo units. They may include barcodes, addresses, handling symbols, and regulatory markings.

definition: Identification markings placed on packages to facilitate handling and verification.
summary: Shipping marks assist in matching cargo to documentation and ensure correct delivery. They are especially important in breakbulk and consolidated shipments.

definition: A document provided by the shipper to a carrier or terminal describing export consignments offered for transport.
summary: The shipping note supplies essential cargo information and supports receipt and liability declarations. It is commonly used in multimodal and terminal operations.

definition: The deficiency between the required quantity and the quantity actually delivered or available.
summary: Shortage may arise from loss, damage, theft, or measurement discrepancies. It is a key consideration in claims handling and inventory control.

definition: A packaging process where heat shrinks plastic film tightly around goods.
summary: Shrink wrapping secures multiple units into a single handling unit and protects cargo during transport. It is commonly used for palletized goods.

definition: Containers or cargo not loaded onto the intended vessel.
summary: Shut-outs occur due to space constraints, operational issues, or documentation problems. The cargo is typically rebooked on a subsequent sailing.

definition: Repeated transport movement between two fixed points over a short route.
summary: Shuttle services are commonly used between ports, terminals, depots, or distribution centers. They support high-frequency, predictable cargo flows.

definition: A short railway track connected to a main line to serve a facility or industrial area.
summary: Sidings enable direct rail access for loading and unloading goods. They reduce handling costs and improve logistical efficiency.

definition: The modeling of real-world processes to study the impact of changing variables.
summary: Simulation is used in logistics and transport planning to evaluate scenarios, optimize decisions, and manage risk without disrupting actual operations.

definition: An economic area allowing free movement of goods, services, capital, and persons.
summary: The European Single Market came into force in 1993 and eliminated customs declarations for intra-community trade. It significantly reduced trade barriers among member states.

definition: A road trailer designed specifically to carry shipping containers.
summary: Skeleton trailers consist of a minimal frame and wheel set to support container corner castings. They are widely used for port and inland container haulage.

definition: Timber or steel supports placed beneath cargo to allow handling and securing.
summary: Skids facilitate forklift access and improve cargo stability during lifting, stowage, and lashing. They are commonly used for heavy or irregular cargo.

definition: A sleeping compartment installed behind or integrated into a truck cab.
summary: Sleepers enable long-haul drivers to rest between driving periods. They support regulatory compliance with driving and rest time rules.

definition: A pair of drivers alternating between driving and resting.
summary: Sleeper teams maximize vehicle utilization and reduce transit times on long-distance routes. This method is common in time-critical road transport.

definition: An adjustable axle assembly allowing fore-and-aft repositioning on a trailer.
summary: Sliding tandems are used to balance axle loads and comply with legal weight limits. They increase operational flexibility in road transport.

definition: A flexible lifting device made from chain, wire rope, or synthetic material.
summary: Slings are used in cargo handling to lift and secure loads safely. Selection depends on load weight, shape, and handling method.

definition: The space on board a vessel allocated to one TEU.
summary: Slots are an administrative and commercial unit used in container shipping. They support capacity planning, allocation, and chartering arrangements.

definition: A charter agreement granting access to a specified number of container slots.
summary: Slot charters allow carriers to expand network coverage without operating vessels. They are common in alliances and feeder arrangements.

definition: An endorsement confirming that cargo has been loaded onto a vessel.
summary: The SOB notation is applied to bills of lading and is critical for payment under letters of credit. It evidences completion of loading.

definition: A container owned by the shipper rather than the carrier.
summary: SOC equipment provides flexibility and may reduce leasing costs. Responsibility for maintenance and repositioning rests with the owner.

definition: A chronological record of events during a vessel’s port stay.
summary: The SOF is used to calculate laytime, demurrage, and dispatch. It is jointly reviewed by ship and terminal representatives.

definition: A voyage charter covering only part of a vessel’s carrying capacity.
summary: Space charters provide flexibility for charterers without committing to a full vessel. They are used for project, bulk, and containerized cargo.

definition: A rate applicable to the carriage of designated commodities.
summary: SCRs reflect the handling, density, or risk characteristics of particular goods. They are commonly used in air cargo tariffs.

definition: The maximum speed a vehicle can achieve under defined conditions.
summary: Speedability depends on engine power, weight, aerodynamics, and road gradient. It is relevant in vehicle performance and route planning.

definition: The reinforcement of circular tanks to prevent deformation during transport.
summary: Spidering uses crossbeams to stabilize tank structures under load. The reinforcement resembles a spider pattern and protects structural integrity.

definition: The transport stretch between a hub and one of the consignees or consignors served by that hub.
summary: In hub-and-spoke logistics networks, a spoke represents the feeder leg connecting the central hub to outlying origins or destinations. Spokes enable consolidation, efficient routing, and cost control by channeling flows through a central node.

definition: The lowest temperature at which a substance ignites spontaneously without an external ignition source.
summary: This parameter is critical in the handling, storage, and transport of hazardous and bulk commodities. It is used in safety assessments, cargo declarations, and compliance with fire and dangerous goods regulations.

definition: A market for unplanned purchases conducted outside long-term contract terms.
summary: Spot market transactions are typically one-off and driven by immediate demand or supply imbalances. In logistics and shipping, spot markets are common for freight, capacity, and commodities during volatile conditions.

definition: A device used for lifting containers or unitized cargo during handling operations.
summary: Spreaders attach to cranes and ensure safe, balanced lifting of standardized units such as containers. Variants include fixed, telescopic, and twin-lift spreaders used at ports and terminals.

term: Signing and Releasing Bill of Lading
definition: A procedure allowing a Bill of Lading to be signed and released without full physical presentation.
summary: SRBL is used to accelerate document flow and cargo release, particularly in liner shipping. It reduces administrative delays while maintaining contractual validity between parties.

definition: A charter party or contract term excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays from time calculations.
summary: SSHEX is commonly applied in laytime and demurrage calculations. It protects charterers from time counting during non-working days as defined in the contract.

definition: A charter party or contract term including Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays in time calculations.
summary: SSHINC accelerates laytime consumption by counting all calendar days. It is often negotiated in busy ports or tight vessel schedules.

definition: The ability of a vessel to return to its upright position after being displaced by external forces.
summary: Vessel stability depends on factors such as metacentric height, cargo weight, and distribution. Continuous monitoring during loading and discharging is essential to ensure seaworthiness and safety.

definition: An identifiable group of containers stowed in an orderly manner at a terminal or depot.
summary: Stacks are used to organize containers within yards, freight stations, and depots. Efficient stacking improves space utilization and handling productivity.

definition: The act of placing boxes, bags, containers, or similar items on top of one another.
summary: Stacking is a fundamental warehouse and terminal activity affecting storage density and cargo safety. Improper stacking can lead to cargo damage or handling inefficiencies.

definition: The total weight of containers and cargo within a specific stack or row.
summary: Stackweight is monitored to ensure ground bearing capacity and equipment limits are not exceeded. It is particularly relevant in container terminals and on board vessels.

definition: Agreed protocols and specifications enabling interoperability between systems, products, or organizations.
summary: Standards support compatibility across vendors and industries, especially in logistics and e-commerce. XML-based standards and initiatives such as BizTalk, OBI, and RosettaNet are widely referenced.

definition: Pre-established estimates of the cost of performing an operation under defined conditions.
summary: Standard costs are used for planning, budgeting, and performance measurement. They form the basis for variance analysis and operational control.

definition: A system used in the United States to classify companies by industry type.
summary: SIC codes support statistical analysis, regulatory reporting, and market research. Although partly replaced by NAICS, SIC remains in use in many datasets.

definition: A defined building block describing a service or shipment product with an associated standard cost.
summary: SPMs link business offerings to operational execution. They serve as an interface between commercial management and operations planning.

definition: The process of verifying whether standards and specifications are viable and implementable.
summary: Standards testing ensures that national, international, or military specifications can be applied in practice. It supports compliance, safety, and interoperability objectives.

definition: The right-hand side of a vessel when facing forward.
summary: Starboard is a fundamental nautical reference used in navigation, stowage, and collision avoidance. It is paired with port to describe vessel orientation.

definition: A term meaning subject to sufficient cargo availability, and also referring to the foremost part of a vessel’s bow.
summary: In chartering, STEM is used to qualify cargo commitments. In nautical terminology, it also describes a structural part of the ship.

definition: The management function of directing empty containers to demand locations using forecasting tools.
summary: Container steering minimizes repositioning costs and equipment shortages. Software systems support predictive allocation based on trade flows and inventory levels.

definition: The aftermost part of a vessel.
summary: The stern houses key structural and navigational elements such as the rudder and propeller. It is a standard reference point in ship design and operations.

definition: The ability of a system or service to retain participants over time.
summary: In commercial and logistics platforms, stickiness reflects switching costs and customer lifetime value. High stickiness indicates strong user dependence and loyalty.

definition: Materials within a supply chain expressed in quantities, locations, or values.
summary: Stock represents tied-up capital and service capability. Effective stock management balances availability, cost, and risk.

definition: The systematic administration of stock levels with respect to quantity.
summary: Stock control ensures continuity of supply while minimizing excess inventory. It relies on forecasting, reorder policies, and performance monitoring.

definition: A unit of measurement and identification used to record stock items.
summary: SKUs enable precise tracking, replenishment, and valuation of inventory. They are central to warehouse management systems and ERP platforms.

definition: A system assigning names or numbers to all storage locations within a warehouse.
summary: Stock locator systems improve picking accuracy and space utilization. They are foundational to modern warehouse operations.

definition: A designated point in the supply chain where materials are held available.
summary: Stock points buffer variability between supply and demand. Their placement affects service levels and total logistics cost.

definition: A record showing the quantity and transaction history of a stock item.
summary: Stock records support replenishment decisions and audit control. Accuracy is essential for reliable inventory management.

definition: The activity of placing goods into a store or the condition of being stored.
summary: Storage provides temporal utility by holding goods until needed. It is a core logistics function performed in warehouses and terminals.

definition: A fee levied for keeping goods in storage.
summary: Storage charges compensate for space usage, handling, and facility costs. They are typically time-based and contractually defined.

definition: Provisions and supplies required for operating a vessel.
summary: Stores include fuel, food, spare parts, and consumables. Proper management is essential for voyage continuity and compliance.

definition: The placement and securing of cargo on board a vessel, aircraft, or in a container.
summary: Correct stowage ensures safety, stability, and cargo integrity. It follows regulatory, structural, and operational constraints.

definition: The ratio of cargo volume to weight used to determine space requirements.
summary: Stowage factor is critical in vessel planning and freight calculations. It influences how much cargo can be loaded into available space.

definition: Mandatory directions provided by the shipper regarding cargo stowage.
summary: These instructions address safety, compatibility, and handling requirements. Compliance reduces risk of damage and regulatory breaches.

definition: A plan showing the location of all consignments on board a vessel.
summary: Stowage plans guide stevedores and officers during loading and discharge. They support stability, efficiency, and port rotation requirements.

definition: A person who hides on board a vessel or aircraft to obtain free passage.
summary: Stowaways pose security, legal, and safety risks. Their presence triggers reporting obligations and potential delays.

definition: A wheeled vehicle designed to lift and transport containers within its framework.
summary: Straddle carriers are widely used in container terminals for horizontal transport and stacking. They provide flexibility and high productivity.

definition: A crane spanning an open area such as roadways or rail tracks.
summary: Straddle cranes are used for lifting and moving heavy loads across fixed paths. They are common in terminals and industrial yards.

definition: A vehicle with a cargo body mounted directly on its chassis.
summary: Straight trucks differ from tractor-trailer combinations by having a single rigid frame. They are commonly used for regional and urban deliveries.

definition: A distinctive feature of a networked market that compels buyers and sellers to participate by materially reducing transaction friction.
summary: A strange attractor typically removes a key inefficiency such as search, payment delay, or price comparison. Its presence drives liquidity and repeat usage by making participation economically compelling for both sides of the market.

definition: A flexible band made of metal, plastic, or similar material used to secure cargo units together.
summary: Straps are commonly used in cargo securing and unitization to prevent shifting during handling and transport. They are applied across multiple modes including road, sea, and warehousing operations.

definition: The leg or segment between two defined points in a transport movement.
summary: A stretch represents a discrete portion of a journey used for planning, costing, or operational control. Complex movements may be broken into multiple stretches for clarity and optimization.

definition: The process of unloading cargo from a container.
summary: Stripping is typically performed at a container freight station or warehouse. It is the operational reverse of stuffing and may involve segregation, inspection, or consolidation activities.

definition: The process of loading cargo into a container.
summary: Stuffing requires adherence to weight distribution, securing, and stowage instructions. Proper stuffing is critical to cargo safety, container integrity, and vessel stability.

definition: A contractual qualifier indicating dependency upon a stated condition.
summary: The term is commonly used in chartering and commercial agreements. It allows commitments to remain conditional until the specified requirement is fulfilled.

definition: Optimizing a single component of an organization at the expense of overall system performance.
summary: Suboptimising often results in inefficiencies across interconnected functions. Effective supply chain management seeks system-wide optimization rather than isolated gains.

definition: A defined portion of a larger stretch within a transport movement.
summary: Substretches are used when finer operational or analytical distinction is required. They support more granular cost allocation and performance measurement.

definition: A representative appointed to supervise cargo handling operations on behalf of an interested party.
summary: Supercargoes oversee loading, discharge, and cargo care to protect commercial interests. They commonly act for shipowners, charterers, or shippers.

definition: A sequence of activities that move and transform goods while adding value.
summary: The supply chain includes conversion, assembly, movement, and storage processes. Effective coordination across these events determines cost efficiency and service reliability.

definition: The coordinated management of processes involved in producing, transporting, and distributing goods.
summary: Supply chain management integrates suppliers, carriers, and distributors to improve flow and visibility. Digital platforms enable participation regardless of trading partner size.

definition: A vessel used to transport stores and supplies to offshore installations.
summary: These vessels support drilling rigs and platforms with consumables, equipment, and spare parts. Reliability and scheduling are critical due to offshore operational constraints.

definition: An additional charge applied on top of standard freight or service rates.
summary: Surcharges may reflect fuel costs, congestion, risk, or regulatory requirements. They are typically itemized separately from base freight charges.

definition: A formal inspection conducted by a qualified specialist.
summary: Surveys assess condition, compliance, or damage of vessels, cargo, or equipment. Findings often support insurance, regulatory, or contractual decisions.

definition: A qualified professional who conducts surveys and inspections.
summary: Surveyors may represent classification societies, insurers, or authorities. Their reports carry technical and legal significance.

definition: The vessel draft measured upon arrival in salt water.
summary: SWAD is used for stability, loading, and port clearance calculations. It differs from freshwater draft due to density variation.

definition: The vessel draft measured upon departure in salt water.
summary: SWDD confirms compliance with draft restrictions at sailing. It is critical for safety and regulatory clearance.

definition: The costs incurred when changing suppliers, platforms, or marketplaces.
summary: Switching costs may be financial, operational, or informational. High switching costs increase customer retention in business-to-business markets.

definition: A detachable cargo unit without wheels used in European intermodal transport.
summary: Swop bodies allow tractors to exchange units without waiting for loading or discharge. They are designed for road and rail use, not for sea transport.

definition: The enhanced result achieved through the combined action of multiple parties.
summary: Synergy occurs when collaboration produces outcomes greater than individual efforts. It is a central objective in integrated logistics and supply chains.

definition: A set of connected elements that interact with each other and their environment.
summary: Systems are defined by relationships, dependencies, and feedback loops. Logistics and supply chains function as systems rather than isolated activities.

definition: A European Community customs status assigned to goods that are not in free circulation.
summary: T1 goods remain under customs supervision while moving within or across customs territories. This status is commonly used for transit movements pending clearance, duty payment, or re-export.

definition: A European Community customs status assigned to goods that are in free circulation.
summary: T2 goods have cleared customs formalities and may move freely within the customs territory. This code is frequently used in intra-community transport documentation.

definition: A person responsible for recording cargo quantities and condition during loading or discharge.
summary: The tallyman provides an independent count of cargo items and notes visible damage. These records support cargo claims, disputes, and operational accountability.

definition: A tank surrounded by a container-sized framework designed for transporting liquids or gases in bulk.
summary: Tank containers are used for chemicals, food-grade liquids, and gases. They allow intermodal transport while maintaining containment integrity and safety compliance.

definition: A vessel specifically designed to carry liquid cargo in bulk.
summary: Tankers transport commodities such as crude oil, petroleum products, and chemicals. Their design emphasizes cargo segregation, pumping systems, and spill prevention.

definition: The mass of an empty container including all permanently attached fittings and appliances.
summary: Tare mass is used for weight calculations, payload planning, and regulatory compliance. It is synonymous with tare weight of container.

definition: The weight of an empty container including fittings and equipment in normal operating condition.
summary: Tare weight is critical for determining gross and net cargo weights. Accurate tare values are required for safe stowage and transport documentation.

definition: A published schedule of rates, charges, and applicable transport conditions.
summary: Tariffs define pricing structures and commercial terms for transport services. They support transparency and consistency in freight billing.

definition: A waterproof sheet used to protect cargo from moisture and weather exposure.
summary: Tarpaulins are commonly applied to breakbulk and deck cargo. They provide temporary protection during storage or transit.

definition: A structured classification system that groups items based on defined relationships.
summary: Taxonomies support data organization, searchability, and standardization. They are often used alongside ontologies in information systems.

definition: A placeholder term indicating that a name or party will be designated later.
summary: TBN is frequently used in chartering and contracts when details are pending. It allows agreements to proceed while retaining flexibility.

definition: A charter arrangement where a vessel is hired for a specified period.
summary: Under a time charter, owners retain responsibility for technical management and crewing. Charterers control commercial employment within agreed limits.

definition: The formal contract governing the terms of a time charter.
summary: A time charter party defines hire rate, duration, obligations, and liabilities. It serves as the legal framework for vessel employment.

definition: A facility located at the end or along a transport line where cargo is handled and serviced.
